H0633.emploi: The word appears only six times, all in chapter 6 of Daniel, during the episode of the lions' den. It specifically designates the royal edict that the ministers of Darius the Mede ask the king to promulgate, which prohibits all subjects from praying for thirty days, except to the king himself. The word recurs at each stage of the drama: the proposal of the edict (v. 7), its drafting (v. 8-9), its invocation against Daniel (v. 12-13), and finally the affirmation of its irrevocable character (v. 15). The "prohibition" is always linked to the sovereignty of the king and the immutability of the Persian law.
H0633.portee: This story shows how a human ordinance, even absolutist, cannot bind the conscience of the believer who obeys God. Daniel refuses to comply with the king's prohibition to remain faithful to his prayer. The reader learns that the decrees of men, however solemn they may be, are nothing compared to the obedience owed to God alone.

sens: King of Assyria in the 7th century BC, son of Sennacherib
H0634.detail: Esarhaddon was an Assyrian king who reigned in the 7th century BC. He was the son of Sennacherib, the powerful king of Assyria who besieged Jerusalem. After Sennacherib was assassinated by two of his sons, Adrammelech and Sharezer, in the temple of his god Nisroch, it was Esarhaddon who succeeded him on the throne of Assyria (2 Kings 19:37 and Isaiah 37:38). He also appears in the history of the reconstruction of the temple in Jerusalem after the exile: colonists he had brought up to Samaria come to offer their help to the returning Israelites, invoking their worship of the God of Israel since the time of Esarhaddon (Ezra 4:2).
H0634.origine: His Assyrian name means "Ashur has given a brother," Ashur being the main god of Assyria. Esarhaddon is known in secular history as a powerful king who consolidated the Assyrian empire and led several military campaigns. The Bible mentions him mainly in connection with his succession of Sennacherib and his role in the politics of the ancient Near East.
H0634.emploi: Esarhaddon is mentioned three times in the Bible (2 Kings 19:37, Isaiah 37:38, and Ezra 4:2), always by his full name "Esarhaddon." In the first two passages (which recount the same event), he is presented as the son of Sennacherib who takes power after his father's assassination. In Ezra 4:2, he is mentioned as the ruler who had deported and resettled populations in Samaria, which contextualizes the arrival of these colonists during the time of the reconstruction of the temple.
H0634.portee: Esarhaddon embodies the continuity of Assyrian power against Israel, despite the death of Sennacherib. His reign reminds the Israelites that even after divine judgments, the powers of the world continue to dominate until the time set by God. The mention of his policy of deportation and resettlement shows how God used even pagan kings to fulfill His purposes toward His people.

sens: Jewish woman of the tribe of Benjamin, daughter of Abihail
Cousin and adopted daughter of Mordecai
Queen of Persia, wife of King Ahasuerus
Heroine who saved the Jewish people from planned destruction
H0635.detail: 1. Esther is a young Jewish woman born during the exile, daughter of Abihail and deceased parents. Adopted by her cousin Mordecai, she also bears the Hebrew name Hadassah ("myrtle"), but the text regularly calls her Esther (Esther 2:7). 2. Mordecai raises her as his own daughter; she grows up in her cousin's house, concealing her Jewish identity from everyone, and she obeys his counsel (Esther 2:10, 4:10-17). 3. Noticed for her beauty and grace, she becomes queen of Persia when King Ahasuerus chooses her to replace the repudiated queen Vashti (Esther 2:16-17). 4. In the face of Haman's plot to destroy all the Jews in the kingdom, Esther risks her own life by presenting herself to the king without being summoned, then reveals Haman's hidden identity and secures the annulment of the murderous decree (Esther 7:1-8, 8:1-8). She then becomes the instrument of the miraculous deliverance of her people.
H0635.origine: The name Esther means "star" in Persian (according to the ancient definition) or could be related to the goddess Ishtar; it replaces the Jewish name Hadassah. The biblical text plays on this duality: an identity hidden under a Persian name, revealing the central theme of the book — God acts in silence through ordinary characters to save His people.
H0635.emploi: Esther appears 52 times in the book that bears her name, from chapter 2 to chapter 9. She enters the scene as a young girl without parents, becomes queen by the king's grace, and then shifts from anonymity and submission to decisive action when she discovers Haman's plot (Esther 4:10-17). The narrative shows her gradual transformation: first discreet and obedient to Mordecai, she gains courage and speaks to the king to defend her people (Esther 5:1-7, 7:3-6). After Haman's downfall and the Jews' victory, she plays an active role in establishing the feast of Purim (Esther 9:29-32).
H0635.portee: The story of Esther teaches that God governs events even when His name is never mentioned in the text. It shows how an ordinary woman, placed in a position of responsibility, can choose to risk her life to defend her people and her faith (Esther 4:15-16: "If I perish, I perish"). For the Christian reader, Esther illustrates the divine origin of the circumstances that save God's people and reminds us that faithfulness and courage, even when hidden and humble at first, produce a deliverance that no earthly power could prevent.

sens: raw material of wood, as a construction material
beam or piece of wood
object or idol carved from wood
wood used in punishment
H0636.detail:
1. Wood is the raw material obtained from trees, used as a solid and durable construction material. In the reconstruction of the Temple in Jerusalem, wood is placed in the walls alongside hewn stones to form the structure of the building (Ezra 5:8 and 6:4).
2. A beam or piece of wood is a large structural element, shaped to be inserted into a construction or used in punishment. In Darius's decree, there is mention of tearing a piece of wood from a house to attach a guilty person (Ezra 6:11).
3. Wood can refer to an object or an idol carved from wood. The Babylonians worshiped wooden gods, just as they did gods of gold, silver, or stone — inanimate objects incapable of seeing, hearing, or knowing (Daniel 5:4 and 5:23).
4. A piece of wood can serve as a means of corporal punishment: erected like a gallows or a stake, it becomes an instrument of torture reserved for transgressors.
H0636.origine: This Aramaic word is the exact counterpart of the Hebrew word עֵץ (ets), which also means "wood" or "tree." Both terms share the same root and imagery: a solid material, derived from nature, transformed by man for his needs. The Aramaic word אָע appears in the Aramaic sections of the Bible (Ezra and Daniel), where the original Hebrew text shifts to the Aramaic language used during the Persian period.
H0636.emploi: This word appears five times in the Aramaic New Testament, solely in the books of Ezra and Daniel. It first denotes the construction material of the Temple restored under Darius, in association with hewn stone. It can then express wood as an isolated piece, particularly as an instrument of punishment (the wood of a gallows or stake). Finally, it denotes the wooden idols worshiped by the Babylonians, incapable of action or divine perception. In all cases, wood remains an inert material, subject to the will of the one who works it.
H0636.portee: This word reminds us that idols, no matter how beautiful and precious they may seem, are nothing but wood, stone, or metal — lifeless matter, without soul, sense, or power. In contrast to these false gods, the living God who holds the breath and ways of man in His hand is sovereignly superior. The wood of punishment also evokes execution — a reminder that transgressing the king's order leads to death: an image that prefigures the wood of the cross in Jesus Christ.

sens: addition of one fact to another, one person to another
reinforcement of an idea: 'and even', 'much more'
personal participation or implication: 'me too', 'you too'
strengthened affirmation: 'indeed', 'certainly'
H0637.detail:
1. The word introduces a second fact, a second person, to bring them together. In Genesis 3:1, the serpent is described as the most cunning of all the animals; aph adds: God also created the serpent. In Leviticus 26:41, God says that Israel has fallen but 'I also will go against you' — the parallel reinforces the cause-and-effect relationship.

2. It amplifies an affirmation, meaning 'and more', 'much more'. In Genesis 18:23-24, Abraham asks: will you do justice to the righteous and the wicked? Abraham adds: how much more will you do it! This is asking if God will act justly, and even more (aph reinforces the implicit).

3. It marks that the speaker or the interlocutor is personally concerned. In Psalms 108:2 (or 109:1), the psalmist sings and adds 'I too' will make my instruments sound. In 1 Samuel 14:30, Jonathan says 'how much more my people too' would have acted: he himself was participating.

4. Sometimes aph gives a tone of insistence, of obviousness: 'certainly', 'for sure'. In Job 40:3, Job wonders if he should answer the Lord or remain silent — aph emphasizes the implicit of judgment.
H0637.origine: The Hebrew word aph literally means 'nose' or 'anger' (the image of the nose that 'trembles' with rage), but in this sense, it is a conjunctive particle inherited from ancient Semitic languages. It expresses addition, accumulation, reinforcement. Aramaic uses the same form (H0638). The transition from 'nose' to 'also' occurred through the idea of 'surplus', of 'what exceeds', because the nose protrudes from the face.
H0637.emploi: This word appears 123 times in the Hebrew Bible. It is very common in the poetic books (Psalms, Job) where it amplifies religious affirmations: 'God is holy, and even the heavens cannot contain him' (2 Chronicles 6:18). In the Law (Leviticus, Deuteronomy), it links promises and threats: 'I will strike you, and even seven times' (Leviticus 26:28). In historical and sapiential narratives, it allows for comparisons: 'Abraham also' believed, 'Job also' suffers. As one moves from narrative to poetry, aph transitions from a simple conjunction 'and' to a marker of logical or emotional reinforcement.
H0637.portee: This word invites the reader to see the links of the divine Word: what God promises to one people extends to another; what he demands from the righteous also applies to the believer today. Aph teaches the universality of grace and judgment. It pushes us to read biblical promises not as isolated, but as a continuous chain in which we too are called to participate.

sens: Marks the addition, the addition to what has just been said
Marks the reinforced negation in a negative sentence
Can express a concession or a restriction
H0638.detail:
1. The word simply marks that something is added to what precedes: 'we also asked for their names' (Ezra 5:10) means that in addition to what has already been done, this question has been added. It is the idea of a natural addition to a list.
2. In a sentence that already contains a negation, 'also' or 'more' reinforces the no: 'before you, I have done nothing wrong either, O king' (Daniel 6:22) means 'you too must recognize that I have done nothing wrong' — the addition of the word extends the negation to another person or circumstance.
3. Sometimes it expresses a restriction or a slight concession, qualifying what has just been stated: 'furthermore, the utensils will be returned' (Ezra 6:5) introduces an additional detail in a list of actions.
H0638.origine: It is the Aramaic corresponding to the Hebrew word aph (אַף, H0637). The Hebrew word primarily means 'nose' or 'face', but its meaning of 'also' or 'again' comes from the idea of addition or surplus — adding something is in a sense placing it 'in addition'. The same word is found in the Aramaic sections of Daniel and Ezra.
H0638.emploi: This word appears only four times in biblical Aramaic, all in the books of Ezra and Daniel. It functions as a coordinating conjunction or an adverb to join statements. In Ezra 5:10, it adds one action to another. In Ezra 5:14 and 6:5, it fits into a narrative of successive royal actions ('also the king did...'). In Daniel 6:22, it appears in a negative sentence to reinforce and extend the negation. It is a common word in Aramaic, but infrequent in the preserved biblical text.
H0638.portee: For the reader, this small word shows how the Bible recounts facts: by adding detail after detail, event after event, which creates an impression of completeness and faithful testimony. In Daniel 6:22, the reinforcement of the negation by 'also' emphasizes that Daniel's conscience is clear both before God and before the king — no trace of guilt anywhere. This is a feature of biblical narration: nothing is hidden, everything adds to the truth.

sens: Feeling of rage, intense fury that overtakes a person
Angry disposition, habitual tendency toward anger
Punishment, severe judgment that expresses divine anger
Irritation, displeasure of a lesser intensity
H0639G.detail: 1. Anger is primarily a violent feeling that consumes the one who experiences it: the Hebrew word aph literally evokes the nose and nostrils, for when one is angry, one breathes heavily, the nostrils dilate. When the anger of God 'burns' (Deuteronomy 29:27), it is like a fire that unleashes. 2. Anger can also describe a character trait, a propensity for rage that resides in someone: Simeon and Levi are 'terrible in their anger' (Genesis 49:6-7), which shows that they are of a fiery nature. 3. The word also designates the fearsome judgment by which God punishes sin: the anger of the Lord that burns against the land (Deuteronomy 29:27) or that ignites like fire in Jacob (Lamentations 2:3) is this destructive power that he unleashes on those who disobey him. 4. More rarely, it expresses simple irritation, a less violent displeasure: when Rachel says to Jacob 'Am I in the place of God?' after reproaching him for her barrenness, it is her anger in the sense of a strong protest (Genesis 30:2).
H0639G.origine: The Hebrew word aph comes from a root that means 'nose' or 'nostrils'. It is a very vivid image: anger is first seen in the face, in the panting breath of the one who is inflamed. When it is said 'the anger burns' (literally 'his nose burns'), one imagines the nostrils dilating and reddening under the effect of rage. In the Bible, 'the anger of God' often translates this same root applied to God: it describes his judgment as a personal and visceral reaction against sin.
H0639G.emploi: The word appears 219 times in the Old Testament, primarily in the books of Moses, the Kings, and the Psalms. It is used for human anger (that of Pharaoh, Esau, Simeon, and Levi) and especially for the anger of God, which constitutes the dominant meaning. Divine anger is presented as a response to disobedience: it burns when Israel idolizes (Exodus 32:10-12), when the people murmur in the desert (Numbers 11:1-10), when Israel transgresses the covenant (Joshua 7:1). It manifests through punishment: death, slavery, destruction. God can also 'withdraw' his anger and return to pity (Psalms 85:4, Nehemiah 9:17).
H0639G.portee: For the believer, understanding this word first reminds us that God is not indifferent to sin: his anger expresses his holiness and justice. It is a serious warning against disobedience and unfaithfulness. But the Bible also shows that God's anger can be appeased: it is not uncontrolled rage, but a personal reaction of the holy God. This tension between God's judgment and mercy is at the heart of the biblical message.

sens: Opening of the nose through which one breathes
Nose, part of the face
Breath, breath of life
Anger, fury (image of smoke from the nostrils)
H0639H.detail:
1. The nostrils are the two openings through which one breathes. This is the most concrete and literal meaning of the word. It is clearly seen when the Lord God "breathed into his nostrils the breath of life" (Genesis 2:7) to animate the first man, or when the waters of the flood rise to the nostrils of the creatures (Genesis 7:22).
2. The word also designates the entire nose, the visible part of the face. The romantic poetry of the Song of Songs praises the beloved's nose: "Your nose is like the tower of Lebanon" (Song of Songs 7:5), comparing it to a majestic edifice.
3. The nostrils become the image of breathing and vital breath. Job confesses: "As long as my breath is in me, and the breath of God is in my nostrils" (Job 27:3), meaning as long as he remains alive.
4. Finally, the smoke that escapes from the nostrils symbolizes divine anger: "By the blast of your nostrils" (Psalms 18:16) evokes the eruption of God's anger, and putting a hook in the nostrils of an enemy (Isaiah 37:29) means to subjugate him by brutal domination.
H0639H.origine: The word אַף (aph) primarily designates the physical organ of the nose and nostrils. Its first image is that of the breath and air that comes out of the nose when one breathes. This is why it naturally comes to also mean vital breath and breathing itself, and then to symbolize anger (like the smoke that comes from someone's nostrils in rage). This progression from the concrete to the figurative is very characteristic of Hebrew.
H0639H.emploi: The word appears 27 times in the Old Testament, especially in the poetic and prophetic books. It is first used in the anatomical sense: to breathe through the nostrils (Genesis 2:7, Job 27:3), to have something in the nostrils (Numbers 11:20). Very often, it designates the nose as part of the face in descriptions or poetic comparisons (Song of Songs 7:5, Proverbs 11:22). But its richest usage is figurative: God's nostrils express His fearsome breath (Psalms 18:16, Isaiah 37:29), and placing a hook in someone's nostrils means to completely dominate him (Isaiah 37:29, 2 Kings 19:28). The context determines whether the word simply evokes the living body or the terrible power of God.
H0639H.portee: This word reminds us that life comes from the divine breath breathed into our nostrils. Every breath is a renewed gift from God. The image of God's nostrils also expresses that His anger is real and terrible: it is not cold and abstract, but alive and powerful, like the air we breathe. For those who follow Jesus, meditating on the breath of life invites gratitude towards the Creator who sustains us every moment.

sens: The visible part of the human body that bears features and emotions
The nose or nostrils
The physical presence of someone, their appearance
The expression of anger or fury
H0639I.detail:
1. The face is the front of the body, the seat of features and expressions. It identifies a person and reveals their emotions. When David prostrates "his face to the ground" (1 Samuel 20:41), he completely lowers himself, showing the deepest respect.
2. The nose or nostrils are sometimes referred to by this same word, as they are part of it. This is a common synecdoche: the part for the whole.
3. The face also represents the entire presence of the person. To appear "face to face" means to be in direct presence. When one prostrates, they hide their face as a sign of humility or reverence before an authority or before God (2 Samuel 14:33).
4. By extension, the face expresses a person's anger or fury, their passionate ardor — an idea that the word also carries etymologically.
H0639I.origine: The Hebrew word "aph" primarily designates the nose and nostrils by their visible physical aspect. It derives from a root that evokes breath and ardor. The same word has taken on the secondary meaning of "anger," because anger "burns" on the face, inflaming the features — this image is found in expressions like "to inflame the face" or "to breathe heavily with fury." In Greek, this word is often rendered by "prosôpon" (face, presence) or by expressions related to anger.
H0639I.emploi: The word appears 24 times in the provided biblical usages, mostly in accounts of respect and prostration. Genesis and Samuel contain the most occurrences. Its usage nuances: in the primary sense, it simply designates the physical face (Genesis 3:19, where sweat flows from the face); in the secondary sense, it expresses the posture of humility when one prostrates "face to the ground" before a king or authority (1 Samuel 20:41, 25:41, 2 Samuel 14:33); in these cases, showing one's face or hiding it means exposing oneself or lowering oneself. The forms "face to" regularly return to depict complete prostration. The word also acquires a passionate hue when associated with anger or imposing presence.
H0639I.portee: This word invites the reader to meditate on the posture of humility before God and authority. When one prostrates "face to the ground," they acknowledge their smallness and dependence. It is also a reminder that the face carries the expression of who we are: our emotions, our respect, or our pride are read on our features. For the Christian, presenting oneself "face to face" before God means coming with sincerity and transparency.

sens: To securely attach a garment or object around the body using a belt or band
To clothe someone with an important piece of clothing, notably the priest's ephod
H0640.detail:
1. The verb primarily designates the action of girding, that is, securely attaching a piece of clothing or an accessory around the body. It is the image of a belt that tightens and holds in place. In Exodus 29:5, Aaron is "girded" with the belt of the ephod to ensure that this priestly garment remains well fixed on his body.
2. The word is also used for the complete act of clothing someone with a solemn piece of clothing, especially the ephod. It is less about the action of girding alone than the entirety of the dressing gesture. In Leviticus 8:7, the text states that Aaron is "girded," but in this context of consecration, the action encompasses the entire official preparation of the priest before his service.
H0640.origine: The verb comes from a Hebrew root that carries the primary image of tightening, enclosing. It is directly related to the word "ephod" (Hebrew: אֵפוֹד, ephod), the sleeveless priestly garment that was girded around the body. In fact, the verb "gird" and the noun "ephod" share the same sphere: to gird is to place the ephod in position and secure it with a belt. It is a very specialized word in the vocabulary of Israelite worship.
H0640.emploi: The verb appears only twice in the Bible, both in passages that describe the ritual dressing of the high priest. In Exodus 29:5, it is Moses who is tasked with girding Aaron with the priestly garment before his inauguration. In Leviticus 8:7, the text recounts how this command was executed during the actual consecration ceremony. Both times, it involves clothing the ephod and fixing its belt, a foundational gesture of the priest's service before God. It is an official, symbolic act that marks the beginning of the priest's function.
H0640.portee: This verb reminds us that becoming a priest of God means being clothed, that is, set apart and equipped for the sacred function. The ephod was not just a simple garment: it carried the Urim and Thummim, through which God manifested Himself. To gird someone with such a robe, therefore, was to place them under divine authority and invest them with a responsibility of mediation between God and the people. For the reader, this illustrates the seriousness of the calling and the necessity to prepare oneself, to allow oneself to be "clothed" by God.

sens: Man of the people of Israel at the time of the Exodus from Egypt and the desert
H0641.detail: 1. Ephod is a leader of the people of Israel, father of Hanniel, who is among the princes of the twelve tribes. He lived during the time when Moses led the people in the desert after the Exodus from Egypt.
H0641.origine: The name Ephod appears only once in the biblical text. Although it is phonetically close to the Hebrew word "ephod" (אֵפוֹד) which designates a special garment or belt, it is here a proper name, that is, a true personal name borne by this man.
H0641.emploi: Ephod is mentioned only once, in Numbers 34:23, in the context of the division of the land of Canaan. Moses lists the leaders who are to supervise this distribution to the different tribes. Hanniel, his son, is designated as the prince representing the tribe of Manasseh during this allocation. The absence of other mentions suggests that this man held a particular administrative role at this crucial moment in Israel's history.

sens: Priestly garment worn on the shoulders by the priest
Cape or linen mantle for the ordinary priest
More precious garment for the high priest, woven with gold and purple with a breastplate adorned with precious stones
Metal covering or plating over idols
H0642.detail:
1. The ephod is primarily a garment that the priest wears on his shoulders, like a cape or mantle. It is a functional garment that distinguishes him in his service at the sanctuary. Exodus 28:8 and 39:5 describe how it is secured by a precious belt of gold and blue, purple, and scarlet threads.
2. For the ordinary priest, the ephod is made of simple white linen, a basic fabric suitable for his role as a minister of worship.
3. For the high priest, the ephod becomes much richer and more complex: it is woven with gold mixed with blue, purple, and scarlet threads, and it bears on the chest a breastplate adorned with twelve precious stones engraved with the names of the tribes. It is a garment of glory and authority.
4. The word also designates a metal covering or plating, like that which covers idols (Isaiah 30:22): a simple layer of metal applied to a statue to decorate it or present it as precious.
H0642.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of girding or fastening. The ephod is thus named because it envelops the priest, particularly his shoulders and chest, and is secured by a belt. It is a garment that binds and gathers several elements — pieces of fabric, stones, gold — into a single sacred adornment.
H0642.emploi: The word appears three times in the provided usages. Twice in Exodus 28 and 39, where it concerns elements of the priest's garment in the construction of the tabernacle: the focus is on the belt that secures the ephod and the precious materials that compose it. Once in Isaiah 30:22, where it describes the covering of the idols that the Judeans must reject as a defilement. The word thus changes context: from the holy garment of the priest to the vain worship of false gods. In both cases, it refers to what envelops, girds, or covers a person or object.
H0642.portee: The ephod reminds the believer that serving God requires visible preparation and separation. For the priest, this precious garment is also a burden: he must reflect the holiness of the one he represents before the Lord. When Isaiah mentions the ephod of the idols, he highlights the contrast: false gods deserve only empty and deceptive coverings, while the worship of the true God is expressed through a splendor that serves a purpose.

sens: Royal or princely building, seat of power
Sumptuous residence of a sovereign
Court or residence of the king
H0643.detail:
1. The palace is the grand building where a king or prince lives and reigns, the center of his power and administration. It is a magnificent structure, built for the glory of the one who resides there. In Daniel 11:45, the expression "will pitch the tents of his palace" refers to the place where the king of the North will establish himself, his royal headquarters between the seas.
2. The word also evokes the luxurious dwelling, the seat of royal authority from which decisions governing the kingdom are made. It is the place of the throne and court, where the powerful of the kingdom gather.
3. By extension, it can also refer to the court itself, the entirety of those who revolve around the sovereign in his official residence.
H0643.origine: The Hebrew word אַפֶּדֶן (appéden) is probably borrowed from Persian or an ancient Near Eastern language. It enters the vocabulary of late Hebrew, particularly in the passages of Daniel that refer to foreign kingdoms. The basic image is that of a grand construction, a fortified building where the king establishes his power.
H0643.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Daniel 11:45, where it describes the palace that the king of the North will establish "between the seas," in a glorious and sacred place. This unique usage shows that the term belongs to the language of late prophecy, when Hebrew borrows from the vocabularies of the empires that dominated the ancient world. In this context, the palace is not just a royal house: it is the visible manifestation of the power and ambition of a king who claims to reign over the nations.
H0643.portee: This word reminds the believer that empires and their rulers, despite their magnificence and pride, are subject to the limits that God sets for them. The palace of the king of the North, even erected in a seemingly invincible place, remains fragile and temporary. The Bible thus shows that no human dwelling, however splendid, can escape the judgment of God.

sens: Prepare bread or cakes by subjecting them to the heat of the oven
One whose profession is to bake bread
To be subjected to baking in the oven
H0644.detail:
1. To bake bread or cakes: this means to subject the dough to the heat of the oven to transform it into baked and edible bread. Lot experiences this when the angels visit: "he baked unleavened bread" (Genesis 19:3). At the Exodus from Egypt, the Hebrews "baked cakes made without leaven" (Exodus 12:39), pressed for time and unable to wait for the dough to rise.
2. The baker, one whose profession is to bake bread: the "chief baker" of Pharaoh (Genesis 40:5) is an important royal officer. The king of Egypt can "lift up the head of the chief baker" (Genesis 40:20) — that is, promote him. The word designates both the action and the one who performs it.
3. To be baked in the oven: the offerings "baked in the oven" (Leviticus 7:9) or the bread of offering "baked" (Leviticus 24:5) refer to what has undergone baking. It is the passive state of the same process.
H0644.origine: The Hebrew verb אָפָה comes from a root that evokes the idea of shaping or transforming by heat. The root is simple and primitive in the language, directly linking the action of baking to the transformation of the dough. The context of biblical narratives shows that baking in the oven was a common and important practice in the daily and cultic life of Israel.
H0644.emploi: This verb appears 24 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in historical narratives and laws regarding offerings. It is found in Genesis (the story of Lot and the dreams of Pharaoh's baker), in Exodus and Leviticus (sacrificial ordinances and prescription of the breads), in 1 Samuel, and in the prophets (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Hosea). The verb designates sometimes the concrete action of baking (Genesis 19:3), sometimes the profession of the one who bakes (Genesis 40:5), sometimes the state of the baked result (Leviticus 7:9). Hosea uses it figuratively: "Like an oven heated by the baker" (Hosea 7:4), an image of inner passion and plots.
H0644.portee: This word reminds us that daily food — bread — requires patient work, a regular transformation. For Israel, the baked offerings "baked" remind that worship is an ordered, careful work offered to God. Hosea uses the image of the oven heating to speak of moral corruption: a heat that destroys. The baked bread also evokes human fragility and dependence on divine provision.

sens: Marks logical consequence or the continuation of an idea
Introduces a question that requires justification or confirmation
Expresses a conclusion or a supported affirmation
Links a condition to its result
H0645.detail:
1. The word "therefore" connects two ideas: one states a fact, the other draws the logical conclusion. For example, when Israel says to his sons, "Since it is necessary, do this" (Genesis 43:11), the "therefore" indicates that the action must follow from the established necessity.
2. Very often, "therefore" introduces a question that awaits an explanation or refutes something. Isaac asks, "Who is therefore the one who has hunted game?" (Genesis 27:33) — he seeks to understand how Esau could already be back, as something does not add up.
3. The word also supports an affirmation: "Know then that it is God who pursues me" (Job 19:6) — it adds weight to what has just been stated, like an accent of certainty.
4. In conditional structures ("if... then"), "therefore" expresses the expected result of the supposition, linking two moments of reasoning.
H0645.origine: This Hebrew word comes from a root expressing "where" and the present moment. It is related to expressions of place and time in Hebrew. Its use has expanded to mark the logical link between two propositions, acting as a hinge in discourse. It is a natural rhetorical tool in Hebrew for constructing clear arguments.
H0645.emploi: The word appears 15 times in the Old Testament, mainly in poetic and narrative books (Genesis, Job, Judges, Isaiah). In Genesis 27:33 and 43:11, it serves to express astonishment or to introduce a directive. In Job (9:24, 19:6, 24:25), it reinforces the argument of the speaking character, giving authority to his statement. In Judges 9:38, it restarts a challenge in a conflicting situation. The word functions everywhere as a quick and incisive connector of thought, marking that what follows derives from what precedes.
H0645.portee: This word, simple in appearance, reveals how the Bible reasons: it never states facts in isolation but always chains them to their consequences or causes. For the reader, "therefore" invites one to follow divine logic: actions have consequences, words engage a response, justice has a result. It is a lesson in coherence: God declares nothing in vain.

sens: Sleeveless priestly garment worn on the shoulders
Garment of the high priest, adorned with precious stones and gold
Object of worship or divination in local sanctuaries
H0646.detail:
1. The ephod is a white linen garment worn by ordinary priests during service at the tabernacle. It is a type of sleeveless cape or apron that rests on the shoulders, held by bands. In Exodus 28:4, it is part of the set of priestly garments that Moses is commanded to make.
2. The high priest wore a much richer ephod: woven of gold, purple, scarlet, and fine linen, with shoulder pieces adorned with onyx stones engraved with the names of the tribes (Exodus 28:6-12). The breastplate, this square adorned with twelve precious stones to consult God's will, was securely attached to it by gold rings (Exodus 28:26-27).
3. In the later times of the book of Judges, the ephod becomes an object of worship in private or local sanctuaries, sometimes associated with idols (Judges 17:5; 18:14-18). This diverted worship retains only the symbol of the priestly garment, without the authority of the tabernacle or the presence of the living God.
H0646.origine: The Hebrew word אֵפוֹד (ephod) originally designates a garment worn on the shoulders. Its exact etymology remains debated, but the word refers to the idea of covering or dressing. In Exodus 28, Moses is commanded to create this ephod as a visible symbol of priestly authority and the link between the people and the Lord. The garment bears engraved the twelve tribes of Israel, showing that the high priest carries them before God.
H0646.emploi: The word appears 39 times, mainly in Exodus (chapters 25, 28-29, 35, 39) where it describes in detail the making and structure of the priestly ephod. In Leviticus 8:7, Aaron puts on the ephod during his inauguration. Throughout 1 Samuel, the ephod of the tabernacle is worn by the priests and allows them to consult God (1 Samuel 23:6-9, 30:7). But from Judges 17-18, the term also applies to religious objects created without divine authority, showing a degradation: the ephod becomes a cultic ornament separated from its true function.
H0646.portee: The ephod reminds the believer that true worship is ordained by God Himself in its details. It is a symbol of mediation: the high priest bore the twelve tribes engraved on his shoulder pieces, showing that his service was for all the people. The breastplate with the Urim and Thummim attached to the ephod represents the ability to know divine will. In contrast, the ephods of the Judges show the danger of religion without scriptural authority: religious forms are created that resemble the truth but are devoid of divine power and direction.

sens: Ancestor of King Saul, from the tribe of Benjamin
H0647.detail: Aphiach is a man from the tribe of Benjamin mentioned only once in the Bible, as an ancestor of King Saul. He appears in Saul's genealogy in 1 Samuel 9:1, where the paternal lineage of the king is traced: Saul was the son of Kish, who was the son of Abiel, himself the son of Zeror, son of Becorath, son of Aphiach. This name in a genealogy testifies to the importance that the Bible attaches to the origins of the kings of Israel and their rooting in one of the twelve tribes.
H0647.origine: The name Aphiach means "I will breathe" or "I make blow" (from the Hebrew root evoking breath or wind). It is a theophoric name that expresses an action or a divine blessing, like many Hebrew names of that time.
H0647.emploi: Aphiach is mentioned only once in the entire Bible, in 1 Samuel 9:1. He appears in the genealogical list that establishes the ancestors of King Saul at the time of the founding of the monarchy in Israel. The text places him among the men of value and strength from the tribe of Benjamin, highlighting the weight and honor of this royal lineage.

sens: That arrives, occurs, or matures later than usual
That blooms or develops at the end of the season
H0648.detail:
1. This word describes something that happens or manifests later than expected. In the text of Exodus 9:32, wheat and spelt are called "late" because they have not yet matured when the other crops were struck by the plagues of Egypt: these grains grew more slowly and reached maturity later in the season.
2. The word evokes the idea of development or growth that extends until the end of the development period. It is the opposite of early crops that mature quickly: late varieties need more time to reach their full maturity.
H0648.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of prolongation or delay. It is related to Arabic terms meaning "to be late" or "to delay." The basic image is that of time passing: a late thing is something that requires more time to come about or reach its end.
H0648.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Exodus 9:32. It is used to explain why wheat and spelt escaped the plagues that struck Egypt: because of their late nature, these crops had not yet reached the stage where they could have been completely destroyed by hail and other plagues. This context shows that "late" applies here to cultivated plant varieties characterized by a longer growth cycle.
H0648.portee: This word reminds us that God knows the rhythm of created things — including the natural cycle of crops. It shows how even seemingly insignificant details of nature come into play during the unfolding of the plagues of Egypt: nothing escapes divine sovereignty.

sens: Man of the tribe of Judah, son of Nadab
H0649.detail: Appaïm is a man belonging to the tribe of Judah, son of Nadab. He appears in the genealogy of Judah, where he is mentioned alongside his brother Seled, who died without children. Appaïm had a son named Jischeï, who continued the lineage (1 Chronicles 2:30-31).
H0649.origine: The name Appaïm literally means "nostrils" in Hebrew, which can evoke an image of life or breath — a poetic meaning that fits well with ancient names. He appears in the genealogies of the clan of Nadab, himself the son of Jerahmeel, placing Appaïm within the genealogical lines of the tribe of Judah.
H0649.emploi: Appaïm is mentioned only twice in the Bible, both in 1 Chronicles 2, in the detailed genealogy of the tribe of Judah. He is presented as the son of Nadab and the father of Jischeï. These genealogical verses remind us of the importance of genealogies for Israel after the exile, which reconstructed family ties and tribal heritage.

sens: Watercourse where a stream flows
Gully or narrow valley
Hollow or cavity (figurative sense)
H0650.detail:
1. The bed of a river or stream is the channel that the water has carved into the ground. It is the natural passage where water normally flows. In 2 Samuel 22:16, during the threat of the Lord, "the bed of the sea appeared," meaning that the seabed was uncovered — the water was removed from the path where it usually flowed.
2. A gully is a deep and narrow valley, carved by erosion, often in mountainous or rugged terrain. Ezekiel 32:6 speaks of "ravines" that will be filled, images of these natural hollows in the land. Ezekiel 36:4 mentions the "streams" in a context of mountains and valleys, designating all the small waterways or beds that crisscross the mountainous landscape of Israel.
3. The word also applies figuratively to any hollow or cavity: in Job 40:13, the "tubes" of the crocodile refer to the hollow bones of this animal, which are like channels in the flesh.
H0650.origine: The Hebrew word אָפִיק comes from a root that evokes the idea of digging or forming a channel. It properly designates what has been dug — the bed formed by the passage of water. The same word is used for valleys and gullies, as they are also hollows in the land. The figurative sense (cavity of bone) naturally extends this image of empty and hollow space.
H0650.emploi: This word appears nineteen times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the poetic (Psalms, Job) and prophetic (Isaiah, Ezekiel, Joel) books. It primarily designates the beds of rivers and streams: in Psalms 42:2, the deer longs for streams of water, evoking the small beds where water accumulates. Isaiah 8:7 speaks of the bed of the river that the king of Assyria surpasses by overflowing. It is also used for the gullies and valleys of the mountainous terrain: Ezekiel 36:6 addresses the "streams" along with the mountains, showing that the word includes all waterways and their beds. Finally, the figurative sense appears in Job 40:13 with the "tubes" of brass of the crocodile, where the word designates the hollow bones.
H0650.portee: This word reminds the reader that God orders creation — the waters have their paths, the mountains their valleys. It also illustrates the abundance of life: animals and plants seek water, which follows its natural bed to nourish them. It is an invitation to recognize how God maintains order and life in His creation.

sens: Absence of light, deep darkness
Dark and threatening character
State of confusion or moral trouble
H0651.detail: 1. The word primarily describes physical darkness, the absence of light: a dark place where nothing can be seen. In Amos 5:20, the prophet speaks of the day of the Lord, calling it "dark" — not cheerful and bright, but dark and without luster, like a covered day that brings fear rather than hope. 2. Darkness takes on a moral and spiritual hue: it expresses what is threatening, frightening, what hides danger. The day of the Lord is dreadful precisely because it is "dark," enveloped in a threat that cannot be escaped. 3. Darkness can also symbolize ignorance or moral trouble — the absence of clarity in discernment and direction from God.
H0651.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that means "to be dark." It belongs to the family of terms that describe darkness and gloom, common in the Bible to express either a physical reality or a spiritual state of confusion or separation from God. In the Greek Old Testament, this type of word corresponds to Greek terms that speak of darkness and the absence of divine light.
H0651.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Amos 5:20. The prophet Amos reproaches the people of Israel for hoping in the day of the Lord as if it would bring deliverance and salvation, whereas it will instead be a day of darkness and gloom, filled with divine judgment. The context shows that this word characterizes a fearful event, devoid of joyful promise for those who do not seek justice.
H0651.portee: This word from the prophet reminds us that God's judgment is not a distant abstraction, but a reality that can be terrible for those who reject it. For the believer, it invites us not to be deluded about divine promises: the presence of God brings salvation, but it also judges evil. The image of darkness helps us discern between comforting appearances and the dreadful truth of what we await.

sens: Absence of light, physical darkness
Dark area, place hidden from light
Misfortune, distress, absence of help
Spiritual wandering, ignorance of good
H0652.detail:
1. The word first designates physical darkness, the absence of light — like night or an underground place. Job 28:3 speaks of a man who explores "the stones hidden in darkness": it is the simple idea of a place where light does not penetrate.
2. It also applies to a state of solitude and danger: Job 10:22 describes a "land of deep darkness, where the shadow of death and confusion reign." Darkness becomes the symbol of a hostile and terrifying place.
3. Figuratively, darkness represents misfortune and distress. Job 30:26 says: "I waited for happiness, and misfortune came; I hoped for light, and darkness came" — here, darkness is the image of disaster that engulfs.
4. The word rises to a spiritual sense: darkness symbolizes moral wandering, ignorance of good, life far from God. Psalms 11:2 speaks of shooting "in the shadow at those whose heart is right" — the shadow becomes the place of ambush and cunning.
H0652.origine: The Hebrew word אֹפֶל comes from a root that evokes darkening and obscuring. It belongs to the family of words describing the absence or lack of light. The starting image is purely physical — the absence of day — but it naturally extends to hidden realities, danger, and misfortune. In Hebrew, darkness and light form a fundamental contrast, figuratively representing order and chaos, good and evil, life and death.
H0652.emploi: The word appears 8 times in the Old Testament, mainly in Job and the Psalms. Job often returns to it to express his anguish: the night he curses (Job 3:6), the underground land of shadows (Job 10:22), the darkness that envelops him (Job 23:17). Psalm 11 uses it to depict the ambush of the wicked, who acts hidden in the shadow. Everywhere, the word oscillates between the physical sense (the darkness of the mine or night) and the spiritual or emotional sense (misfortune, suffering, wandering). Especially in Job, "darkness" designates less a place than a state — that of one who is stripped of all help, of all hope of light.
H0652.portee: This word reminds the believer that light and darkness are never neutral in the Bible: they embody spiritual realities. Fleeing darkness and walking in the light is choosing between two worlds — that of life in God and that of wandering. For a reader grappling with suffering (like Job), the word provides language: the darkness he endures is real, deep, terrifying, and it can be named.

sens: Absence of light, thick darkness
Twilight, dusk
Misfortune, calamity
Wickedness, malice
H0653.detail:
1. Darkness is primarily the total or nearly total absence of light: it is the image of the nine plagues of darkness that covered the land of Egypt (Exodus 10:22), or the twilight where the seducer lurks for his prey (Proverbs 7:9). The blind person groping in the darkness of day represents complete helplessness (Deuteronomy 28:29).
2. Darkness also refers to literal or fixed darkness: the dark time of night and twilight, when one can no longer see their way.
3. The Bible uses this word for misfortune and calamity: the way of the wicked is darkness because they do not see the sin that causes them to fall (Proverbs 4:19), and Isaiah announces that darkness and distress will invade the unfaithful land (Isaiah 8:22).
4. Darkness also becomes the image of wickedness itself: those who live far from God walk in the darkness of evil.
H0653.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that first evokes the idea of being "thick" or "dense." Darkness is a thickness that obscures and oppresses: it envelops everything like a veil or a cover, preventing one from seeing and breathing freely. This connection to "thickness" appears in the translations of the Segond which speaks of "thick darkness." The idea transposes to misfortune and sin: evil also "thickens" the heart and darkens the soul.
H0653.emploi: This word appears ten times in the Hebrew Bible, concentrated mainly in passages that describe the condition of the unfortunate, the sinner, or the punished people. Exodus uses it for the plagues of Egypt: a physical, visible, incomprehensible darkness. The wisdom of Proverbs and Isaiah makes it the image of the fate of the wicked and those who stray from God. Isaiah 58:10 reverses the image: righteousness brings back light in place of darkness. Other prophets (Joel, Zephaniah) use it to describe the Day of the Lord as a time of judgment and thick darkness.
H0653.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us that sin is not a simple deviation: it is a darkness that envelops, paralyzes, and misleads. But Isaiah 58:10 also offers a promise: by giving and serving, one brings back the light, dispelling the darkness. This image challenges the Christian not to live in the darkness of evil or indifference, but to seek the light of God and good.

sens: A man from the tribe of Judah, living during the time of the divided monarchy
H0654.detail: Ephlal is a name that appears in the genealogy of the tribe of Judah, at the time when the kingdom of Israel was divided between the North and the South. He is the son of Zabad and the father of Obed, thus fitting into a long chain of descendants from the patriarch Perez. Although little known as an individual, his existence is attested and recorded in the sacred genealogical records of God's people.
H0654.origine: The name Ephlal means "intercessor" according to ancient etymological tradition. This meaning refers to the idea of a person who intercedes or intervenes on behalf of others. The name belongs to the long list of Hebrew names that expressed a quality or function, often related to prayers and relationships with God.
H0654.emploi: Ephlal appears only once in the Scriptures, in 1 Chronicles 2:37, in the detailed genealogy of the tribe of Judah. He is mentioned simply as a link in a family chain: Zabad begot Ephlal, and Ephlal begot Obed. This mention is part of the great genealogical record of God's people, which traces back to Perez, son of Judah, and bears witness to the continuity of the promised lineage.
H0654.portee: The mention of Ephlal, although brief, reminds us that God knows every man and woman of His people, even those whose names are not associated with any great event. His inscription in the sacred genealogy affirms that every life, every generation has its place in God's plan and in the history of salvation.

sens: The appropriate moment, the opportune occasion, the suitable timing
The circumstance or situation that makes an action or word relevant
What is adapted to the conditions of the moment
H0655.detail:
1. Timing primarily refers to the right moment, the occasion that comes at the right time — not too early, not too late. When Solomon speaks of a word said "at the right time," he evokes a word that arrives exactly when it is needed, like a golden apple shining on a silver plate (Proverbs 25:11): it is the striking contrast between the present and its context that gives it beauty.
2. In a broader sense, the word refers to the circumstance or condition of the moment — what makes the action opportune. A word "at the right time" is not only well said; it is said in the exact conditions where it bears fruit, where it is received, where it soothes or encourages.
3. Thus, it is a word that speaks of correctness and harmony: the word finds its weight and strength not only through its content but through its moment of utterance. Saying the right thing at the wrong time wastes it; at the right time, it is a gift.
H0655.origine: The Hebrew word אֹפֶן (ophèn) comes from a root that evokes the idea of turning, changing, positioning — hence the image of circumstance or moment as a "position" where the word is placed. The same word can designate a wheel or a cycle, reminding us that time turns and returns: there is a time for everything, and the art is to recognize when the wheel stops at the right place.
H0655.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible in this sense, in the Proverbs of Solomon. It is a term of practical wisdom: Solomon teaches that the beauty and effectiveness of a word depend on its timing, that is, on the timing and contextual relevance. It is a lesson on the weight of words — not only their content but their moment, their place, their circumstance.
H0655.portee: For the believer, this verse reminds us that wisdom consists in knowing not only what to say but when and how to say it. A right word at the wrong time can hurt or be lost; at the right time, it becomes precious like gold. It is an invitation to listen to the Holy Spirit, not only about the content of our words but about their timing — to recognize when the moment has come to speak and when to be silent.

sens: To come to an end, to disappear completely
To be exhausted, to have no reserve left
To no longer exist, to be annihilated
H0656.detail:
1. The word describes the action of coming to an end, disappearing completely: what existed no longer exists. It is the image of something that stops definitively. In Genesis 47:15, the money of the land "fails" — there is no more at all, everything has been consumed.

2. It also means to be exhausted or emptied of its content, to have no resources left. Joseph tells the Egyptians: "if the money fails," meaning if there is nothing left to give (Genesis 47:16).

3. The word can express the annihilation or disappearance of a more serious reality: in Isaiah 16:4, "oppression will cease," the devastator "will disappear" — evil powers are erased, they have no more existence or power.
H0656.origine: The Hebrew word aphones comes from a root that evokes the fundamental idea of finitude and limitation: something comes to its end, exhausted or destroyed. This root appears in other words designating the end or absence. The basic image is that of a reserve that is completely drained, of a force that is extinguished.
H0656.emploi: The verb appears five times in the Hebrew Bible, concentrated in a few key contexts. In Genesis 47, repeated twice, it describes the exhaustion of Egyptian money during the famine: a concrete, economic situation where resources disappear. In Isaiah (16:4 and 29:20), the word takes on a spiritual and political significance: oppression ceases, the oppressors and mockers are annihilated. One use in the Psalms (77:9) applies it to divine mercy — "Has His mercy ceased?" — questioning whether God abandons His people.
H0656.portee: This word speaks to those who suffer from hardship, famine, or oppression: it reminds us that all that is evil is not eternal, that it comes to an end. It also invites the believer to see that what seems infinite — money, power, cruelty — is exhausted and dies. It is a promise of hope: God will never cease His mercy, but all that oppresses will eventually cease.

sens: Limit, edge, or end of an expanse (land, sea, territory)
Cessation, stop, disappearance of something
Absolute negation: nothing, no one, none
Complement that reinforces a negation or restriction
H0657A.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to the edges or limits of a region: "He will rule from sea to sea, and from the river to the ends of the earth" (Psalms 72:8). It is encountered when discussing the borders, ends of the world, or limits of a territory.
2. It also expresses cessation, annihilation: "All its princes will be annihilated" (Isaiah 34:12). The word conveys the idea that something comes to an end, disappears, or completely fades away.
3. Because of this idea of disappearance, it becomes a way to express total absence, nothingness: "For I am God, and there is no other; I am God, and there is none like me" (Isaiah 46:9) — literally "and there is no other" (no other exists).
4. Often, it reinforces a negation or nuances a restriction: "However, there will be no poor among you" (Deuteronomy 15:4). Here, it softens or clarifies the scope of a statement.
H0657A.origine: The Hebrew root can refer to the idea of finishing, ceasing. The word expresses absence through the idea of limit or exhaustion: what reaches its extremity no longer truly exists. This is why it can denote both a spatial limit (the end of a land) and a negation (nothing, no one). The word family in Hebrew has few variants, but the central image remains that of culmination and end.
H0657A.emploi: The word appears 42 times in biblical Hebrew, mainly in Psalms, Isaiah, and the historical books. When it describes a spatial extremity, it concerns the borders of the earth or a domain: "from the river to the ends of the earth" (Psalms 72:8), "from one sea to another" (Psalms 2:8). When it pertains to disappearance or absence, it often accompanies verbs of annihilation or is included in negative phrases: "there is no other" (Isaiah 46:9), "without the effort of any hand" (Daniel 8:25). In some cases, it softens a statement or limits its scope, like a polite restriction: "However, there will be no poor among you" (Deuteronomy 15:4).
H0657A.portee: This word reminds us that God alone reaches the ends of the earth and that nothing escapes His gaze. It also expresses the vanity of what is human without Him: everything fades away, everything becomes nothing. For the reader, it invites seeking not at the ends of the world, but with God, the lasting source of all good.

sens: The joint or bone that connects the leg to the foot
The lower extremity of the leg, just above the foot
H0657B.detail:
1. The word refers to the ankle joint, the bony and articulated area that connects the leg to the foot. It is the thinnest part of the leg, before the toes. In Ezekiel 47:3, the prophet must cross water that rises "to the ankles": the water level barely reaches this joint.
2. By extension, the word also applies to the lower extremity of the leg itself, the lowest area of the limb that can be submerged or touched.
H0657B.origine: The Hebrew word אֹפֶס (o.phes) evokes the two extremities of the body or an object — an idea rendered by "soles" in English. The word comes from a root that expresses the idea of end, limit, or what terminates. In Hebrew, an ankle is literally what terminates the leg.
H0657B.emploi: The word appears only once in the preserved Hebrew biblical text, in Ezekiel 47:3. In this passage, the prophet crosses a miraculous stream that flows from the restored temple: the water rises gradually, first to the ankles, then to the knees, then to the hips, and finally becomes an unpassable river. The mention of the ankles serves to describe the first stage of immersion, marking the beginning of the water's invasion.
H0657B.portee: This concrete anatomical detail in Ezekiel's vision emphasizes the reality and progression of God's miraculous transformation of the world. Starting from the ankles and rising, the text makes the scene vivid and measurable, inviting the reader to visualize the increasing extent of divine power.

sens: Location in Judah, between Soco and Azekah, about 25 kilometers southwest of Jerusalem
H0658.detail: 1. It is a place in the mountainous region of Judah, known as the site where the Philistines gathered to confront Israel. Its Hebrew name literally means "border of blood" or "edge of blood," alluding to the carnage of battles. It is here that the famous encounter between David and Goliath took place (1 Samuel 17:1).
H0658.origine: The Hebrew name Ephes-Dammim means "border of blood": ephes means "limit" or "edge," and dammim means "blood." This place was located in the border area where the armies of the Philistines and Israel clashed, hence a name that evokes the bloody battles of this contested region.
H0658.emploi: This name appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Samuel 17:1, to designate the battlefield where the Philistines had stationed themselves in wait. It is the context of the confrontation between David and Goliath, one of the most memorable stories of the Old Testament. The place also has another name, Pas-dammim ("passage of blood"), showing the symbolic importance of blood and combat in biblical geography.
H0658.portee: This place reminds us that Israel's victories did not come from military strength, but from faith in God. It was on this battlefield that David, a simple shepherd without armor or sword, defeated the giant Goliath by trusting in the name of the Lord — a lasting lesson for Christians facing their own giants.

sens: What does not exist, what is empty of reality
What has no value, no price
What is futile, unimportant
What is null, without effect
H0659.detail:
1. Nothingness denotes complete absence, what is nothing: in Isaiah 41:24, idols and their worshippers are called "nothingness," meaning they have no reality or substance compared to God.
2. It is also what has no value or interest: the works of idols are "nothingness," hollow and vain.
3. The word expresses what is despicable and worthy of horror: Scripture says it is an "abomination" to take pleasure in what is nothing.
4. It is what produces no lasting effect: nothingness can offer nothing to the faithful, neither protection nor salvation.
H0659.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a very ancient root that expresses the idea of emptiness and non-existence. It belongs to a semantic field close to words for "nothing" and "vanity," found in other biblical texts. The starting image is that of absolute nothingness, of non-being.
H0659.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Isaiah 41:24. It is used by the prophet to describe the radical impotence of idols before the living God. The context is a trial where God challenges the idols to justify themselves: they are nothingness, their work does not exist, and those who cling to them commit an abomination. The uniqueness of this usage shows the intensity of the judgment the prophet places on idolatry.
H0659.portee: This word reminds Christians that everything that opposes God or turns away from Him has no real substance, despite appearances. It invites not to fear the powers or systems that seem powerful but are empty before the eternal God. It is a call to place trust in the One who truly is, and not in what is nothing.

sens: Venomous snake from Asia and Africa, with a stocky body
Image of evil, sin, and dangerous cunning
Progeny of the wicked, malice that spreads
H0660.detail:
1. The viper is a short and robust venomous snake that lives in the desert regions of the Middle East. It represents an immediate and deadly danger to anyone who encounters it or suffers its bite: in Job 20:16, the text speaks of a man who has sucked the venom of the asp, and whose "the tongue of the viper will kill him," an image of death by poisoning.
2. In the Bible, the viper becomes the image of hidden evil and malice. In Isaiah 30:6, it appears alongside the lion and the flying dragon among the terrifying beasts of the southern desert, symbolizing the perils that threaten God's people.
3. More profoundly, the viper symbolizes the progeny of evil, the malice that begets and spreads. Isaiah 59:5 clearly shows this: "He who eats their eggs dies; and if one breaks them, a viper comes out" — meaning that the eggs of evil give birth to evil, that malice produces deadly fruits.
H0660.origine: The Hebrew word אֶפְעֶה (ephéa) literally designates this specific snake, well identified in the ancient Near East. Its Hebrew name remains focused on the concrete animal, without elaborate etymology. The viper is known to the Hebrews as a fearsome creature of the desert and arid regions, and the Bible quickly uses it as a metaphor for danger that brings death.
H0660.emploi: The word appears three times in the Old Testament, always to evoke the snake itself or its deadly action, but each time in a context of judgment or warning. In Job 20:16, it refers to the punishment of the wicked who poisons himself with his own venom. In Isaiah 30:6, the viper is mentioned in a list of natural plagues threatening Judah. In Isaiah 59:5, it becomes the image of what is born from human malice: the eggs of the wicked produce vipers. The word is used referentially and symbolically, never neutrally: it is always a sign of evil, death, or divine judgment.
H0660.portee: The viper reminds the Christian reader that evil is not an accident or a figment of the imagination, but a concrete and deadly reality — as real and dangerous as a venomous snake. It also teaches that evil begets evil: whoever cultivates malice, cunning, and injustice inevitably brings about destruction, first for themselves. It is a call to spiritual vigilance and a break with sin.

sens: To encircle someone or something on all sides, in a way that encloses or encircles it
To be around something in a way that covers or overwhelms it
To press, squeeze closely, in a sense of danger or distress
H0661.detail:
1. The literal meaning is to completely surround something, as one surrounds a city to take it or isolate it. In Jonah 2:6, the waters and the reeds "surround" Jonah, encircling him from all sides, literally engulfing him.
2. The word also designates the action of being surrounded by a situation that crushes or imprisons you. In Psalms 40:13, the troubles "surround" the psalmist — these are not just distant problems, they surround him, besiege him on all sides, so numerous that he loses courage.
3. By extension, "surround" evokes distress, the anguish that grips you closely. In Psalms 18:5 and 116:3, the cords of death and the torrents of destruction have "surrounded" the psalmist — the image is one of a grip, a trap that tightens.
H0661.origine: The Hebrew verb אָפַף (apheph) comes from a root that fundamentally means "to surround," "to encircle." It expresses the idea of an action that completely envelops you, encircling you on all sides. The word belongs to a small family of terms describing gestures of enclosing or encircling.
H0661.emploi: This verb appears five times in the Hebrew Bible, almost always in contexts of distress or danger. Two parallel passages (2 Samuel 22:5 and Psalms 18:5) show it in the same context: the floods of death and the torrents of destruction surround the one who cries out to God. The psalmist uses this word to express that danger encircles him from all sides, that there is no escape anywhere. In Psalms 40:13 and 116:3, the verb expresses being encircled by troubles and anxieties. Jonah 2:6 uses it to describe how the waters cover and envelop the prophet, surrounding him from the belly of the fish. It is always an image of being seized, pressed, without freedom of movement.
H0661.portee: This word serves to express the concrete experience of spiritual distress: not a distant threat, but a reality that surrounds and grips you. For the believer, "surround" reminds us that in the darkest moments, God sees where we are — surrounded, but not abandoned. That is why the psalmist cries out to the One who can deliver us from this encirclement. The word makes palpable what the suffering one feels: the impression that evil presses in from all sides.

sens: To master one's emotions, inner agitation
To show restraint, not to let feelings explode
To keep silent voluntarily, to refrain from speaking
To use force against oneself, to constrain oneself
H0662.detail:
1. To master one's emotions: it is to hold back an intense emotion that seeks to escape. Joseph in Egypt "could no longer contain himself" before his unknown brothers (Genesis 45:1) — love, joy, and hidden identity were boiling within him to the point that he had to send everyone out to finally reveal himself. Haman also "knew how to contain himself" (Esther 5:10) when he left the king's presence, keeping his impatience within.
2. To show restraint: it is the effort of one who wants to appear self-controlled despite the inner storm. Joseph, "making efforts to contain himself" after washing his face (Genesis 43:31), displays calm while his heart secretly recognizes his brothers.
3. To keep silent, to restrain one's words: the Lord says, "I have long kept silent, I have been quiet, I have contained myself" (Isaiah 42:14), then adds, "I will cry out" — an image of a restraint so long that it becomes painful, followed by an inevitable explosion.
4. To use force against oneself: Saul confesses, "I forced myself and offered the burnt offering" (1 Samuel 13:12), meaning he forced himself to act against his will, constraining himself.
H0662.origine: The Hebrew verb אָפַק (aphaq) comes from a root that originally means "to retain" or "to contain." It is an active verb, which describes the action of one who exerts force. In the reflexive form used here (Hithpael), the subject restrains himself: he inflicts inner violence upon himself. This form expresses the voluntary effort of self-control.
H0662.emploi: This verb appears 7 times in the Bible according to these uses. It mainly occurs in narratives showing characters grappling with their emotions: Joseph mastering his emotion before his brothers (Genesis 43:31; 45:1), Haman maintaining composure despite his irritation (Esther 5:10). Once, Saul uses it to say that he forced himself to offer a sacrifice (1 Samuel 13:12). Finally, the psalmist or the prophet uses it to speak of the Lord who has long restrained Himself (Isaiah 42:14; 63:15; 64:11) — God who could explode with anger but holds back in patience. It is always the effort of one who tames an inner force.
H0662.portee: This word teaches the importance of self-control in spiritual life. Joseph, rather than revealing his identity immediately, contains himself and waits for God's perfect timing — his restraint becomes a sign of wisdom. Conversely, when we see the Lord containing Himself, we discover that divine patience is never indifference, but effort: God holds back His anger out of love. For the believer, this word reminds us that mastering one's emotions is not weakness, but strength.

sens: Canaanite city in Palestine
military encampment site of the Philistines
strategic location near the Jezreel Valley
H0663G.detail:
1. Aphek is a fortified Canaanite city located in the Promised Land. Its name means "enclosure" or "closed place," evoking a fortified site. It is listed among the royal cities defeated during the conquest (Joshua 12:18).
2. The Bible mentions Aphek as a strategic point where the Philistines established their military camps. It is where they gathered before fighting Israel, notably during the battle when the Ark of the Covenant was captured (1 Samuel 4:1).
3. Aphek was also a concentration point for the Philistine military, from which they launched their operations against Israel. It remained an important enemy stronghold in Palestinian geography (1 Samuel 29:1).
H0663G.origine: The name Aphek (אֲפֵק) derives from a Semitic root meaning "enclosure" or "fortification." It designates a closed and defended space, characteristic of the fortified cities of the ancient Levant. This etymology reflects the nature of the city: a fortified urban center capable of serving as a strategic military base for the peoples who controlled it.
H0663G.emploi: Aphek is mentioned three times in the Hebrew Bible, always in connection with the Philistines or the Canaanite conquest. In Joshua 12:18, it is counted among the thirty-one kings of Canaan defeated by Joshua. In 1 Samuel 4:1 and 29:1, it becomes a major Philistine military camp from which they launch their campaigns against Israel during the time of Samuel and Saul. The city embodies the strategic threat that the Philistines posed to Israel during this period of Israelite history.
H0663G.portee: Aphek reminds believers that Israel's victory depended on faithfulness to God, not on military strength or enemy fortifications. The defeats and victories at Aphek illustrate how God governs the history of nations and how Israel, often militarily defeated, was called to place its trust solely in Him.

sens: City of Canaan in the territory of the Phoenicians
Location in the northwest of the Promised Land
H0663H.detail:
1. Aphek is a city of Canaan located in the northwest of the Promised Land, in the coastal region inhabited by the Phoenicians and Canaanites. Its name means "enclosure" or "fortification," which corresponds to its role as a stronghold. It appears in the lists of cities that were to be conquered upon entering Canaan.

2. According to biblical mentions, Aphek was located in the territory assigned to the tribe of Asher, a maritime region in the north. The Israelites were unable to drive out the Canaanite inhabitants, as indicated by the passage in Judges 1:31, which lists the cities from which Asher "did not drive out the inhabitants."
H0663H.origine: The Hebrew name אֲפֵק (aphéq) literally means "enclosure" or "fortified enclosure," suggesting a city surrounded by walls or fortifications. This etymology reflects the strategic importance of the locality. The name also appears in the form Aphik in ancient texts, a minor variant of the same name.
H0663H.emploi: Aphek appears three times in the Hebrew Bible. It is mentioned as a boundary of the Canaanite territory in the land distribution (Joshua 13:4), then listed among the cities in the territory of Asher (Joshua 19:30). It finally appears in the account of the cities that the Israelites were unable to conquer (Judges 1:31), illustrating the initial inability of the tribes to expel all the Canaanites from their assigned territories.

sens: Fortified city in Syria where armies clashed
H0663I.detail: 1. Aphek is a fortified city located in Syrian territory, not far from Israel. It appears as a strategic war location: Ben-Hadad, king of Syria, gathered his troops there (1 Kings 20:26) and took refuge there after his defeat (1 Kings 20:30), while the prophet Elisha announced to the king of Israel a victory against the Syrians (2 Kings 13:17).
H0663I.origine: The name means "enclosure" or "enclosure" in Hebrew, evoking a city closed by walls. The city of Aphek was a strategic crossing or confrontation point between Syria and the territory of Israel, which explains its repeated military importance in biblical accounts.
H0663I.emploi: Aphek is mentioned three times in the two books of Kings, always in the context of wars between Israel and Syria during the reign of Ahab and his son Ahaziah. In 1 Kings 20:26 and 20:30, it is the scene of Ben-Hadad's defeat before Israel: first a gathering point for Syrian troops, then a place of refuge and the final debacle where the wall collapses on the fleeing soldiers. In 2 Kings 13:17, many years later, it is the symbolic place where God promises the king a complete victory against the Syrians. Aphek thus embodies the place where God intervenes to grant victory to Israel.
H0663I.portee: Aphek reminds us that God uses history and geography to accomplish His purposes. The victories announced and realized at Aphek show that even against an organized military power (the Syrians), God grants victory to His people when they act according to His will. It is an encouragement to trust in God's promises rather than in the strength of arms.

sens: Fortified city near Hebron in Judah
H0664.detail: Aphéka is a fortified city in the territory of Judah, mentioned in the list of cities that Joshua distributed to the children of Judah after the conquest of the land (Joshua 15:53). It was located near Hebron, one of the most important cities in the region, in the mountainous area of southern Judah.
H0664.origine: The name Aphéka means "enclosure" or "enclosure," evoking a fortified place. It is a variant of the name of another city called Aphek (אֲפֵק), which shares the same Hebrew root. Several cities bore the name Aphek in Israel; this one was specifically in the territory of Judah.
H0664.emploi: Aphéka appears only once in the Bible, in the list of cities assigned to the tribe of Judah after the conquest of Canaan (Joshua 15). This list enumerates about 115 cities intended to serve as administrative centers and refuge for the Judeans. Its inclusion in this context shows its importance as a place of life and territorial control in the southern region.

sens: Gray and powdery residue that remains after the complete combustion of a material
Visible symbol of mourning, humiliation, and repentance
H0665.detail:
1. Ash is the gray residue that remains after a fire has burned something. It is a fine and light powder. In the Bible, it is notably encountered in relation to sacrifices and purification rituals: the ashes of the red heifer are used to purify the defiled Israelites (Numbers 19:9-10).
2. Ash becomes a gesture and a symbol: when someone suffers or wants to express their humiliation before God, they cover themselves with ash. Abraham says to God, "I am but dust and ashes" (Genesis 18:27), acknowledging his smallness. Tamar, violated and desperate, "put ashes on her head" (2 Samuel 13:19). Job, in his extreme suffering, "sat in ashes" (Job 2:8). This is a gesture of deep emotional significance: ash, which is nothing, represents the annihilation of pride and the acceptance of divine judgment. When Ezekiel mourns Tyre, he says that one will "roll in ashes" (Ezekiel 27:30).
H0665.origine: The Hebrew word אֵפֶר (epher) literally refers to the powdery residue of fire. The image evokes both fragility (ash disperses in the wind) and annihilation (what has burned does not return). In the Old Testament, ash is associated with purification and mourning rites: it is a substance that separates, marks, and purifies. Ash also reminds man of his nothingness: "You are dust, and to dust you shall return" (implicit in biblical imagery).
H0665.emploi: The word appears 22 times in the Old Testament. It is first used in a ritual and legal context: the ashes of the red heifer purify impurities (Numbers 19). It is also heavily used in the context of mourning and repentance: Tamar, Job, Mordecai in Persia, and the inhabitants of Nineveh who repent under Jonah all cover themselves with ash. It is a language of the body, as eloquent as tears. Finally, the word takes on a moral and figurative value: one who "feeds on ashes" (Isaiah 44:20) is one who nourishes themselves with illusions, with vain things. Ash symbolizes what is worthless, what does not last.
H0665.portee: For the reader, ash speaks of two realities: on one hand, it reminds us that all flesh is mortal and fragile, dust destined to return to dust. On the other hand, it is a humble and sincere gesture: covering oneself with ash before God is to acknowledge one's sin without reservation, to accept judgment. This is why true repentance in the Bible is not limited to words; it is expressed through the body, through gestures. Ash invites the believer to sincerity and humility before God.

sens: Fabric or band that covers the eyes
That which hides, conceals, or deceives the gaze
H0666.detail:
1. A fabric or band that is placed over the eyes to cover them and prevent seeing. The prophet in 1 Kings 20:38 puts a bandage over his eyes to disguise himself before the king.
