2. Figuratively, anything that obstructs vision or misleads judgment: that which masks the truth or deceives someone. The bandage removed (1 Kings 20:41), the king recognizes the prophet — revelation replaces illusion.
H0666.origine: The Hebrew word אֲפֵר comes from a root that evokes the idea of covering or wrapping. It concretely refers to what wraps and protects, or what hides. The context of the text shows a practical use: a bandage or veil serving to conceal identity.
H0666.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible, both in 1 Kings 20, in the episode where a prophet disguises himself to approach the king of Israel. In verse 38, he puts on the bandage to avoid being recognized; in verse 41, he removes it to reveal himself. The use is strictly concrete and dramatic: the bandage is the instrument of disguise, and its removal marks the moment of truth.
H0666.portee: This brief narrative teaches that appearances can be deceiving and that the truth ultimately reveals itself. The bandage symbolizes voluntary or imposed blindness; its removal signifies illumination and recognition. For the believer, this reminds us that only God sees clearly and judges justly.

sens: Young bird still dependent on its mother
Young of any species of bird: eagle, songbird, swallow
H0667.detail:
1. The word refers to a bird that has just been born or has not yet reached full development. In Deuteronomy 22:6, the law protects the young birds along with the mother, showing that they are vulnerable and dependent creatures that need parental care to survive.
2. The word applies to all birds without distinction: it can refer to an eagle whose young "drink the blood" of prey (Job 39:33), a swallow that "deposits its young" in a nest (Psalms 84:4), or simple songbirds. It is a generic term for winged offspring.
H0667.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that expresses the idea of youth or smallness. It simply describes what is young in the order of birds, without any particular connotation — it is a descriptive term of the natural state of juvenile dependence.
H0667.emploi: The word appears three times in the Hebrew Bible, always in the plural ("young"). In Deuteronomy 22:6, it is part of a moral law that prohibits taking the mother with her young: this shows the biblical concern for respecting familial bonds and animal reproduction. In Job 39:33, it characterizes the eagle whose young feed on bloody prey, illustrating the natural ferocity of this bird of prey. In Psalms 84:4, the swallow deposits its young near the altars of God, creating a touching image of parental tenderness and trust in God — the psalmist draws a spiritual lesson about attachment to the house of God.
H0667.portee: This word reminds the reader of the vulnerability of new life and the responsibility we have towards creatures. The law of Deuteronomy teaches respect for motherhood and the natural cycle. The image from Psalm 84 invites us to meditate on what truly drives us to seek rest: just as the bird builds its nest and deposits its young safely, the believer's heart seeks its home in God.

sens: Portable seat or bed, closed or open, carried on the shoulders of servants
Luxury vehicle for a high-ranking individual
Mark of royal status and dignity
H0668.detail:
1. A litter is a portable piece of furniture, a kind of bed or seat that bearers hold on their shoulders or arms to transport a person from one place to another. It is a comfortable means of transport, closed or adorned with curtains, which protects the person it carries. Solomon had one made of wood from Lebanon (Song of Solomon 3:9), indicating that it is richly furnished.
2. A litter is a symbol of power and well-being: only kings, great lords, or very high-ranking individuals travel this way. It is a luxury reserved for the elite, marking the distance between the one who rests in it and the people who walk.
3. In the text of the Song, Solomon's litter symbolizes his glorious royalty and opulence: it is one of the splendors by which the king displays his magnificence and love.
H0668.origine: The Hebrew word אַפִּרְיוֹן (appiryôn) is a loanword, probably from the Sanskrit « paryaṅka » or a related language, which referred to this piece of transport furniture in the ancient East. It describes a luxury item known in Egypt, Persia, and India, where kings and dignitaries traveled this way. Greek borrowed it in the form φορεῖον (phoreîon).
H0668.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Song of Solomon 3:9, where it describes the sumptuous litter that King Solomon had made of wood from Lebanon, surrounded by ornaments of gold and silver. This unique context is enough to show that the litter was, in the eyes of the Israelites, a prestigious object associated with royal prestige and the power of the monarch. The term evokes a striking contrast: a piece of furniture that is carried, thus implying a symbolic dominance over those who bear it, and which displays the glory of the one who rests in it.
H0668.portee: For the Christian, this image of the royal litter invites reflection on what royalty, power, and earthly glory mean. In the Song, it expresses the bride's admiration for the king's magnificence, but it also reminds us that these splendors are fleeting. In contrast, Jesus, although the true King, chose to enter Jerusalem on a donkey, not in a precious litter: this underscores the humility of Christ and the different nature of his reign, founded not on luxury or domination, but on service and love.

sens: Son of Joseph and Asenath, Joseph's second son
Tribe of Israel descended from this son
Mountainous territory occupied by this tribe in central Canaan
Sometimes name of the Northern Kingdom, Northern Israel
H0669G.detail:
1. Ephraim is the second son of Joseph, born in Egypt. At his birth, Joseph gives him this name to thank God for making him fruitful despite his sufferings: "God has made me fruitful in the land of my affliction" (Genesis 41:52). Before his death, Joseph blesses Ephraim and Manasseh, his two sons, and adopts them as his own children in the succession of Israel. Remarkably, Joseph crosses his hands while blessing, thereby giving Ephraim, the younger, the greater blessing (Genesis 48:1-20).
2. After the Exodus from Egypt, Ephraim becomes a powerful tribe of Israel. In the census in the desert, it counts 40,500 warriors, making it one of the largest (Numbers 1:32-33). It camps to the east of the Tabernacle and marches under the banner of the camp of Judah.
3. In the distribution of Canaan, the tribe of Ephraim receives a mountainous territory in the center of the land, a region of hills and mountains (Joshua 16:4-10). This territory, called the "mountain of Ephraim," becomes an important religious and military center.
4. Sometimes, the name Ephraim refers to the Northern Kingdom, Northern Israel, particularly in the prophets Hosea and Isaiah. Thus, when Isaiah speaks of the separation of "Ephraim" from Judah, he evokes the political and religious schism that divides the people (Isaiah 7:17).
H0669G.origine: The name "Ephraim" literally means "double fruitfulness" or "he will be doubly fruitful." It comes from the Hebrew root that expresses the idea of fruitfulness and multiplication. Joseph chooses this name to celebrate God's faithfulness in granting him children and unexpected prosperity, despite slavery and suffering in Egypt. The name thus expresses the transformation of pain into blessing: God has made Joseph's life fruitful amid affliction.
H0669G.emploi: Ephraim appears 157 times in the Bible, primarily in historical and prophetic narratives. First mentioned at his birth in Egypt (Genesis 41:52), he is then formally adopted by Jacob as one of his twelve sons (Genesis 48). After the conquest of Canaan, Ephraim becomes a great tribe: it receives a vast territory in the center of the land (Joshua 16-17) and plays a major military role alongside Judah (Judges 7:24; 12:1-6). When the monarchy is divided, Ephraim becomes the dominant tribe of the Northern Kingdom (1 Kings 12:25), and the prophets use its name to refer to the entire Northern Kingdom of Israel, particularly in their calls to repentance (Hosea 6:10; Isaiah 7:17). The term thus evolves from a historical figure to a geographical and political entity, charged with increasing theological significance.
H0669G.portee: The story of Ephraim teaches the believer that God honors his promises and exalts the humble. Despite being the youngest, Ephraim receives the greatest blessing, showing that God does not conform to human conventions to accomplish his plan. For Israel and the Church, Ephraim's fate also reminds us of the cost of division: when the people separate, weakening and exile threaten. The "fruitfulness" that gives Ephraim its name invites every believer to seek a fruitful spiritual life, bearing fruit in faith and obedience.

sens: Major gate of the northern wall of Jerusalem
H0669H.detail: 1. The Ephraim Gate is one of the main gates of Jerusalem, built in the northern wall of the city. It is named after the tribe of Ephraim, which occupied the lands north of Judah, and thus served as access to these northern regions. During the attack by Joash, king of Israel, against Jerusalem, the assailants opened a breach of four hundred cubits in the wall, exactly "from the Ephraim Gate to the Corner Gate" (2 Kings 14:13; 2 Chronicles 25:23), showing that this gate occupied a strategic position in the city's defensive system.
H0669H.origine: The name Ephraim comes from Hebrew and literally means "double heap of ashes" or "I will be doubly fruitful." It was originally the name of an important tribe of Israel (son of Joseph), and then the designation of the Northern Kingdom. The gate of Jerusalem bears this name because it provided access to the region of Ephraim, north of Judah.
H0669H.emploi: The Ephraim Gate appears only twice in the Bible, both in parallel passages (2 Kings 14:13 and 2 Chronicles 25:23), which recount the same event: the attack of Joash of Israel against Amaziah of Judah. In this episode of war between the two kingdoms, this gate appears as a precise topographical landmark to delineate the area where the wall was destroyed. It is an important defensive gate, well known to the ancient inhabitants and readers of these historical accounts.

sens: One of the major gates of Jerusalem during the time of Nehemiah
H0669I.detail: 1. The Gate of Ephraim is one of the main gates of the wall of Jerusalem rebuilt under Nehemiah, after the return from exile. It served as a major passage point in the city and marked an important geographical landmark. It is mentioned during the festivities of the Feast of Tabernacles (Nehemiah 8:16) and in the description of the dedication procession of the walls (Nehemiah 12:39).
H0669I.origine: The name "Ephraim" is not derived here from the eponymous tribe of northern Israel, but its origin remains uncertain. The gate likely bears this name either due to its proximity to a neighborhood or because it commanded a road leading to the territory of Ephraim. Like many gates of Jerusalem, it served to identify and structure access to the fortified city.
H0669I.emploi: This gate is mentioned only twice in the Bible, both in Nehemiah. It appears in the account of the Feast of Tabernacles, where the people gather to celebrate, and in the solemn dedication procession of the walls. These two passages show that it was a well-known gate of ritual importance, serving as a landmark for large gatherings and religious events in the rebuilt Jerusalem.

sens: mountainous region in the center of Palestine
H0669J.detail: 1. Ephraim refers to the mountainous region located in the center of the Promised Land, between Jerusalem and Galilee. In Jeremiah 4:15, the prophet speaks of "the mountain of Ephraim" as a characteristic feature of the landscape.
H0669J.origine: The name Ephraim means "double fruitfulness" or "I will be doubly fruitful." This name comes from a region known for its agricultural fertility, water sources, and wealth in natural resources. It is also the name of Joseph's son and one of the tribes of Israel that bears this name and whose territory covers this mountainous region.
H0669J.emploi: Ephraim designates the mountainous region in the center of the Promised Land. In the provided biblical usage (Jeremiah 4:15), it is mentioned as a major geographical landmark from which calamity is announced, showing that it was a well-known and significant region in the landscape of Israel.

sens: Mountainous region west of the Jordan
Forest or wooded area in this region
H0669K.detail:
1. Ephraim is the name of a mountainous region located in the lands of Israel, west of the Jordan. It takes its name from Ephraim, the son of Joseph, one of the great tribes of Israel that settled there after the conquest of Canaan.
2. The text of 2 Samuel 18:6 speaks of the "forest of Ephraim," indicating that this region was covered with woods and forest vegetation. It was here that an important battle took place during Absalom's revolt against King David.
H0669K.origine: The name Ephraim literally means "double heap of ashes" or evokes the idea of "I will be doubly fruitful." It comes from Ephraim, the son of Joseph, to whom Jacob gave his blessing (see Genesis 48). The term designates both the tribe and the mountainous region it inhabited. When speaking of the "forest of Ephraim," the geographical name is combined with the Hebrew word for forest (ya'ar), creating an expression that precisely designates this wooded area.
H0669K.emploi: Ephraim is used in the Bible to refer to the mountainous region in central Israel. The only usage provided here (2 Samuel 18:6) mentions the "forest of Ephraim" as the site of a crucial battle. It was in this wood that Absalom, the rebellious son of King David, lost his life, marking the end of his rebellion. This forest was dense and constituted difficult terrain for combat, which explains the significant losses during this conflict.
H0669K.portee: For the Christian reader, Ephraim reminds us that the Promised Land had a concrete geography and that God had given each tribe its territory. This region was linked to the memory of Joseph and his descendants, and the events that took place there were part of the history of the chosen people. Recognizing these places helps to better understand the daily life and the political and military issues of God's people in the Old Testament.

sens: Territory or region where the tribe of Ephraim lived
Agricultural and pastoral zone of ancient Israel
Place of gathering and community life
H0669L.detail:
1. Ephraim designates the geographical territory occupied by the tribe of Ephraim in the Promised Land, after the conquest and division of the lands under Joshua. It is a fertile region in the central-northern part of Israel. In 2 Samuel 13:23, King David owned lands near Ephraim where his sheep shearers were located, showing that this region was renowned for its livestock and agricultural resources.
2. The term can also refer to an important domain or territorial possession, such as that owned by the king or his close associates for agricultural and pastoral exploitation. It was an economic center of rural life and production.
H0669L.origine: The name Ephraim comes from the ancient Hebrew language and carries the idea of "double fruitfulness" or "double yield" — as if this land were to bear twice as much harvest, a promise of prosperity. Ephraim was the name of Joseph's younger son, to whom Jacob had granted the blessing of the firstborn; the territory was named after this son. It is a name filled with promise: the one who bears this name is destined to be "doubly fruitful."
H0669L.emploi: Ephraim appears in the Hebrew Bible as the name of the ancestral territory of the eponymous tribe, one of the most powerful in northern Israel. It occupied a strategic and fertile region. The only usage in our texts (2 Samuel 13:23) designates it as a site of royal property, where King David had facilities for sheep shearing — an important pastoral activity at the time. This shows that Ephraim was a region of economic and administrative significance, controlled by the central power.
H0669L.portee: For the biblical reader, Ephraim reminds us that God makes promises of blessing and fruitfulness to His people. This real territory, marked by a prosperous economy, embodied the fulfillment of these divine promises. The name also carries the tension between earthly blessings (fertile land, resources) and faithfulness to God — a central theme in the history of Israel.

sens: Title or official administrative function in the ancient Persian empire
H0670.detail: 1. In the context of the return from exile, "Apharas" designates a charge or an official position in the Persian administration. In Ezra 4:9, this term appears in a list of officials and peoples who oppose the reconstruction of the temple: Rehum is governor, Shimshai is secretary, and "Apharas" appears alongside other titles like "Erec." It is a cog in the bureaucracy of the great king.
H0670.origine: The Hebrew word אֲפָֽרְסָיֵא (apharséya) is a variant form or a transliteration of the Persian word פָּרַס (pares, "Persia"). In this text from Ezra, written during the Persian period, the word can refer either to Persia itself or — and this is the interpretation here — to a Persian-origin administrative title. The exact etymology remains uncertain: some have proposed a root meaning "cause of division," but this remains hypothetical.
H0670.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Ezra 4:9. It is included in a list of officials and peoples from Samaria who write to the king to oppose the reconstruction of the temple in Jerusalem under the reign of Artaxerxes. This list mixes names of peoples (Babylon, Susa, Elam) and presumably administrative titles or functions (like "Apharas" and "Erec"), reflecting the complexity of the Persian empire and its power structures.
H0670.portee: This word reminds us that the people of God, upon their return from exile, had to face hostility from local Persian authorities and neighboring peoples. Despite this organized and administrative opposition, God allowed the temple to be rebuilt. It is a testimony to God's hand accomplishing His purposes despite the obstacles of the world.

sens: Official title or function in the Persian administration
Group of official characters or magistrates
H0671A.detail:
1. Apharsac designates an official title or function in the administration of the Persian Empire. The word appears in the letters addressed to King Darius regarding the reconstruction of the temple in Jerusalem: Thathnai and Shethar-Bozenai are accompanied by their "colleagues of Apharsac" (Ezra 5:6), suggesting a precise administrative role, likely that of a governor or provincial magistrate.
2. The context indicates that Apharsac also refers to the individuals who hold this position — a group of official leaders working together in regional administration, particularly "on this side of the river" (the Euphrates), in the province where Jerusalem is located. This is why the Segond translates this term as the name of a category of official characters or colleagues.
H0671A.origine: The exact etymology of the Aramaic word is uncertain. The ancient definition suggested it might mean "dividers" or "those who cause division," but this interpretation remains hypothetical. The word belongs to the administrative vocabulary of the Persian Empire, likely borrowed from Old Persian. There is no direct Hebrew equivalent, as the term is specifically used to designate a Persian institution.
H0671A.emploi: The word Apharsac appears only twice in the Bible, both in the book of Ezra (5:6 and 6:6), in passages written in Aramaic. It designates official characters who accompany Thathnai, the governor of the region beyond the Euphrates, and who question the authorization to rebuild the temple. These letters to King Darius reflect the bureaucratic Persian administration of the post-exilic period. The exact meaning of the function remains obscure to modern historians, but the context shows that these Apharsac are colleagues of the governors, likely magistrates or administrative advisors.
H0671A.portee: This term bears witness to the historical reality of the Return from Exile under Persian rule. For the Christian reader, it reminds us that even foreign authorities of the empire — seemingly distant and inattentive — can be used by God to enable His people to fulfill their mission of reconstruction. These authentic names and titles anchor biblical history in real history.

sens: Group or administrative function in the Persian Empire
H0671B.detail: 1. This Aramaic term designates a group of people or an administrative function within the Persian Empire. It appears only once in the Bible, in Ezra 4:9, where it is included in a list of peoples or professional bodies participating in a letter addressed to King Artaxerxes. Like many words borrowed from the Persian context, its exact meaning eludes us today.
H0671B.origine: The word is from Aramaic, the language that the Persians used to administer their vast empire. It may be related to other terms designating official functions or social groups in this context. Although hypotheses have been proposed ("dividers" or "deceivers"), none are certain: the word remains an enigma whose precise etymology has been lost.
H0671B.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Ezra 4:9. It is part of a list of groups — governors, secretaries, people from various cities and nations — who rise together to contest the reconstruction project of the temple by the Jews returned from exile. Its context indicates that it refers to a category of people with an administrative or social role in the Persian Empire. The uniqueness of this mention and the absence of parallels in other texts make interpretation difficult.

sens: Wife of Caleb, mother of Hur
Region or locality near Bethel, where Rachel died
Another name for Bethlehem
H0672G.detail:
1. Éphrata was a woman from the tribe of Judah who lived during the time of Egypt and the desert. She was the wife of Caleb and the mother of Hur, from whom several important families of Israel descended (1 Chronicles 2:19).
2. Éphrata also refers to a locality, probably a region or place near Bethel, associated with the death and burial of Rachel.
3. In more recent texts, Éphrata becomes another name for Bethlehem, the city where David was born and, according to prophecy, the Messiah. Micah 5:1 calls Bethlehem "Bethlehem Ephrathah," highlighting its importance despite its smallness among the cities of Judah.
H0672G.origine: The name means "fertile" or "place of fertility" (from the Hebrew root evoking abundance). It initially designated a woman, then a territory, before becoming associated with Bethlehem. The same word can take a suffix to form "Ephrathite," designating an inhabitant or descendant of Éphrata.
H0672G.emploi: This name appears four times in the Bible. Three occurrences concern her as Caleb's wife (1 Chronicles 2:19, 2:50, 4:4), where she is mentioned as the mother of Hur and ancestor of Judah's lineages. A fourth, more famous occurrence, is found in Micah 5:1, where Éphrata is the poetic nickname for Bethlehem, the city of the kings of Judah. This dual reference (woman and place) shows how a personal name could also designate a territory.
H0672G.portee: For the believer, Éphrata/Bethlehem reminds us that God honors humble places and small towns. The mention of Éphrata in Micah 5:1 connects the ancient tribe of Judah to the birth of the Messiah, showing how God prepares and fulfills His promises through the history and geography of Israel.

sens: Region or locality near Bethlehem in the Promised Land
Another name for Bethlehem
H0672H.detail:
1. Éphrata is a region or locality in Canaan, located near Bethlehem. It is where Rachel dies giving birth to Benjamin, and where she is buried on the way (Genesis 35:16-19). The name designates the geographical area immediately surrounding what will become the city of Bethlehem.
2. Éphrata is another name, ancient or parallel, for Bethlehem. The biblical texts explicitly establish this identification: "on the way to Éphrata, which is Bethlehem" (Genesis 35:19; 48:7). In David's time, Éphrata and Bethlehem are mentioned together as the same important place where the Lord is to manifest His strength (Ruth 4:11; Psalms 132:6).
H0672H.origine: The name Éphrata literally means "the fertile" or "the fruitful" (place of fecundity), evoking the richness and productivity of this region. It could also refer to a notion of ash or dust in some ancient etymologies. It is a place rich in history: it is in Éphrata that the royal genealogy of Israel takes root, since Bethlehem will become the city of David and the city of the Messiah.
H0672H.emploi: Éphrata appears five times in the Hebrew Bible. Three occurrences are found in Genesis, associated with the death and burial of Rachel, the mother of Benjamin and Joseph (Genesis 35:16-19; 48:7): these are foundational passages of the patriarchal narrative. Two occurrences are in Ruth and the Psalms, where Éphrata is the place where the story of redemption by Boaz and Ruth is fulfilled, and where the ark of God is to be found. Each time, the Bible equates Éphrata with Bethlehem, either explicitly ("which is Bethlehem") or by context. The name remains that of a region, but it will eventually come to exclusively designate the city that is its heart.
H0672H.portee: Éphrata is the cradle of two essential lineages: that of Rachel, who embodies motherhood and the promise of descendants, and that of David, the anointed king from whom the Messiah will come. For the Christian reader, this place reminds us that Bethlehem did not come from nowhere: it is the culmination of a story of pain, faithfulness, and divine promises. It is there that Christ will be born, in direct continuation of the commitments God made to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

sens: Descendant de la tribu d'Éphraïm
Habitant de la région d'Éphraïm
Habitant de Bethléhem (Éphrata)
H0673G.detail:
1. An Ephraimite is a member of the tribe of Ephraim, one of the twelve tribes of Israel founded by Ephraim, the son of Joseph. This term designates the descendants of this ancestor and the inhabitants of his territory. Thus, in the account of Judges 12:5, during a battle, fugitives are asked: "Are you an Ephraimite?" to identify which tribe they belong to.

2. The term can also simply refer to someone from the mountainous region of Ephraim, like Elkanah in 1 Samuel 1:1, described as "a man from the hill country of Ephraim, named Elkanah."

3. Sometimes, "Ephrathite" also applies to the inhabitants of Bethlehem (also called Ephrath), which could create slight ambiguity. Jeroboam is thus referred to as "an Ephrathite from Zeredah" in 1 Kings 11:26, indicating his place of origin.
H0673G.origine: The word comes from Ephraim (אֶפְרַיִם), the name of Joseph's prominent son, whose Hebrew meaning evokes fertility ("double fruitfulness"). Ephraim was blessed by Jacob and became one of the most powerful tribes in northern Israel. The suffix "-ite" forms the adjective or agent noun, marking belonging or origin: an Ephraimite is literally "one who comes from Ephraim." This same root also designates Bethlehem, formerly called Ephrath.
H0673G.emploi: This word appears three times in the Segond 1910, always to identify a person's tribal or geographical origin. In Judges 12:5, it serves to distinguish fighters during an ambush. In 1 Samuel 1:1, it qualifies Elkanah, the father of Samuel, anchoring his identity in the hill country of Ephraim. In 1 Kings 11:26, it presents Jeroboam before his revolt. In all three cases, the word situates the character in a specific tribal or territorial context, which was crucial for Israelite identity.
H0673G.portee: This term reminds us that Israel's identity is rooted in the tribes, heirs of the promises made to the patriarchs. For the believer, it shows how God has built His people across generations, each occupying their place in the divine plan. It is also an invitation to remember our spiritual origins in Christ.

sens: inhabitant of Bethlehem or the region of Ephrath
H0673H.detail: 1. An Ephrathite is someone from Bethlehem or the region called Ephrath, in Judea. It is a name that simply designates a place of origin, much like saying "Parisian" or "Lyonnais." Elimelech and Jesse, the father of David, are both presented as Ephrathites (Ruth 1:2; 1 Samuel 17:12).
H0673H.origine: The word comes from Ephrath (אֶפְרָת), an ancient name for the region around Bethlehem. This name means "fruitfulness" or "fertility" in Hebrew, evoking the idea of a rich and productive land. The inhabitants of this region were called "Ephrathites." Bethlehem, the city of the kings of Israel, was located in the territory of Ephrath.
H0673H.emploi: The word appears twice in the Bible. In Ruth 1:2, Elimelech and his family are described as Ephrathites of Bethlehem when they leave the famine to go to Moab. In 1 Samuel 17:12, Jesse, the father of David, is also called an Ephrathite of Bethlehem. These two passages show that the term is a simple geographical and social descriptor: it situates a person within their community of origin.
H0673H.portee: This humble geographical detail — "Ephrathite of Bethlehem" — places David in his ordinary genealogy before he becomes king. It reminds us that God often chooses His own from simple people and small towns, and that the most modest origins can precede the greatest destinies.

sens: Wealth and financial resources accumulated by the sovereign
Revenues and taxes paid to the king
H0674.detail:
1. The word designates the wealth, money, and precious goods that a king or the state possesses — what fills the royal coffers. In Ezra 4:13, the adversaries warn the king that the rebuilding of Jerusalem will harm the royal "treasure": if the city rises again, its inhabitants will no longer pay the taxes and dues that once enriched the treasure of the king of Persia.
2. More broadly, the word can also refer to the revenues and taxes themselves — the money that the king collects from his subjects to fill his treasury. The passage in Ezra speaks of the lost money because Jerusalem will no longer be subject to the same tax obligations.
H0674.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes the idea of storing, accumulating, or filling. It concretely refers to a place or quantity where resources are amassed — the treasure as an accumulated reserve. The same family of words appears elsewhere to designate accumulations or deposits, particularly in administrative or fiscal contexts.
H0674.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Ezra 4:13, a passage where the Samaritans and other adversaries write to the king of Persia to dissuade him from allowing the reconstruction of the Temple and the walls of Jerusalem. They warn him: allowing Jerusalem to rise again means losing the taxes and dues that this city was supposed to pay — that is, impoverishing the royal treasury. The context is therefore political and fiscal: the word serves to designate the revenues the king derived from his vassal provinces.
H0674.portee: This passage shows us how human interests — jealousy, competition, love of money — can stand against God's project. The adversaries of Jerusalem bet on the king's selfishness to block the reconstruction. For the Christian reader, it is a reminder that God sometimes acts against seemingly insurmountable obstacles, and that the plans of men, even the most powerful, cannot stop His purpose.

sens: Fils de Gad
Petit-fils de Benjamin
H0675G.detail:
1. Etsbon is a man of the tribe of Gad, living at the time of the Exodus and the sojourn in the desert. He appears in the genealogical list of Genesis 46:16 as one of the seven sons of Gad who go down to Egypt with Jacob.
2. Etsbon is also mentioned in Numbers 26:16, where he is called Ozni. He is one of the ancestors of the Oznites, the family that bears his name among the descendants of Gad.
H0675G.origine: The name Etsbon means "haste to discern" or "I will be enlargement." It is an ancient Hebrew name that fits into the genealogy of the twelve tribes of Israel. The same man is designated by two different names in the biblical texts: Etsbon in Genesis and Ozni in Numbers, which was common in antiquity.
H0675G.emploi: Etsbon appears only once by name in the Bible, in Genesis 46:16, at the time when Jacob and his family go down to Egypt to settle there with Joseph. He is one of the seven sons of Gad listed in this account. In Numbers 26:16, the same character is called Ozni, and he is the head of a genealogical family. These two occurrences designate the same man at two different moments in Israel's history.

sens: Fils de Béla, petit-fils de Benjamin
H0675H.detail: Etsbon is a man of the tribe of Benjamin, mentioned only once in the Bible. He is the son of Bela and the grandson of Benjamin, the patriarch founder of the tribe. At the time of the Exodus and the crossing of the desert, he is one of the family leaders of his tribe and figures among the valiant warriors recorded in the genealogies (1 Chronicles 7:7).
H0675H.origine: The name Etsbon literally means "haste to discern" or "I will be enlargement." It belongs to the Benjamin lineage and marks the genealogical identity of this clan leader in the history of the people of Israel.
H0675H.emploi: Etsbon appears only once in the entire Bible, in 1 Chronicles 7:7. This passage lists the sons of Bela and the notable Benjaminite family leaders — powerful and valiant men whose descendants were counted during a census. His mention, though brief, places him among the respectable figures in the genealogy of Benjamin.

sens: Each of the articulated appendages of the upper or lower limb of the hand or foot
What imitates or evokes the appearance of a finger: a long and slender shape
The ability to act, to intervene with skill or authority
A sign or gesture expressed by the finger
H0676.detail:
1. The finger is literally each of the appendages of the hand or foot: the magicians recognize "the finger of God" in Egypt (Exodus 8:15), an expression that evokes divine power acting directly. The priests dip their finger in the blood of the sacrifices to sprinkle it on the altar (Leviticus 4:17; 16:14), a precise gesture that sanctifies the sanctuary. The toe is also mentioned: the man from Gath had six fingers on each hand and each foot (2 Samuel 21:20).
2. By resemblance of shape, the word applies to long and slender objects: the columns of the temple, eighteen cubits high and about a palm in circumference, are implicitly compared to giant fingers (Jeremiah 52:21).
3. The finger symbolizes the ability to act, to point to something, to exercise authority: God writes the ten words "with the finger of God" on the two tablets (Exodus 31:18), marking His personal imprint in the act. The Lord raises those who accuse others "with their finger" (Isaiah 58:9), meaning those who blame others.
4. The finger can also express an expressive gesture or a sign: one who "makes signs with the fingers" expresses cunning or malice (Proverbs 6:13), and writing the law on the fingers of the heart (Proverbs 7:3) means engraving it in the conscience.
H0676.origine: The Hebrew word אֶצְבַּע (etsba') is ancient and fundamental: it has no clear etymology, but it is found in its Aramaic form as αἴτημα (also etsba'). In the Greek Old Testament, the Greek word δάκτυλος (daktulos) regularly translates it. It is a concrete word that primarily designates the finger as a part of the body, from which all the figurative meanings related to action, power, and gesture arise.
H0676.emploi: The word appears 28 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the Law and wisdom texts. In Leviticus, "finger" is essential to the sacrificial ritual: the priests dip the finger in the blood and sprinkle it seven times (Leviticus 4:17; 16:14), a gesture that purifies and consecrates the altar. In Exodus, the word evokes direct divine power: God writes with His "finger" the ten words (Exodus 31:18), and the magicians recognize the "finger of God" acting in Egypt (Exodus 8:15). In Proverbs and Isaiah, the word becomes figurative: making signs with the finger (Proverbs 6:13), writing the law on the finger of the heart (Proverbs 7:3), or accusing with the finger (Isaiah 58:9). The psalmist contemplates the greatness of God in the face of the vastness of the heavens and asks: what is man that you are mindful of him? (Psalms 8:4).
H0676.portee: The word "finger" reminds the believer of two profound truths. First, God's action is real and tangible: the "finger of God" in Exodus symbolizes a personal and powerful intervention, not abstract. Second, the gesture of the finger invites moral responsibility: we are called to write the Law on our hearts (Proverbs 7:3) and not to accuse with the finger (Isaiah 58:9), but to build up our brothers. It is a word that connects the concrete to the spiritual.

sens: Each of the articulated appendages that terminate the hand or foot
Part of the body that writes, acts, touches
The power or divine action that manifests through signs
Symbol of fragility or strength depending on its substance
H0677.detail:
1. The finger is each of the articulated appendages of the hand or foot: this is the simplest and most concrete meaning. In Nebuchadnezzar's dream (Daniel 2:42), "the toes were partly of iron and partly of clay," which reinforces the image of mixed fragility of the divided kingdom.
2. The finger is what writes and acts: it designates the instrument of action. In Daniel 5:5, "the fingers of a man's hand" write the enigmatic message on the palace wall, a gesture that manifests supernatural presence and divine intervention.
3. The finger can represent the power or divine action that manifests through visible and tangible signs. When God acts "with the tip of His finger," it means His direct and impactful intervention in human history.
4. The finger symbolizes fragility or strength depending on what it is made of: the clay finger is weak and fragile, while the iron finger is hard and powerful. This distinction illustrates how the same kingdom can mix incompatible elements.
H0677.origine: The Hebrew word אֶצְבַּע (ets.ba) literally designates the finger, this small appendage of the body. Its exact etymology is uncertain, but the word is ancient and universal in Semitic languages. In Aramaic, the form is identical, which shows that this vocabulary of the human body has remained stable through the ages and dialects.
H0677.emploi: The word appears three times in the book of Daniel, and all occurrences are from the Aramaic text (chapters 2 and 5). In Daniel 2:41-42, the "fingers" of the feet in the dream symbolize the ten kings or kingdoms to come, a fragile mix of iron and clay. In Daniel 5:5, the "fingers" of a hand mysteriously write on the wall of the Babylonian palace, a miraculous sign of divine intervention judging King Belshazzar. The word oscillates between its simple anatomical meaning and a strong symbolic significance: it designates both a part of the body and the instrument of a superhuman action.
H0677.portee: The finger in the Bible is never an insignificant detail: it is often the vector of a divine action that judges or transforms. Seeing the fingers write God's judgment on the wall should strike the believer's heart: God acts with precision and certainty, and nothing escapes Him. It also reminds us that our whole body, even in its smallest parts, belongs to God and can be the instrument of His will.

sens: Person of high rank, noble condition, distinguished by their position or influence
What is distant, at the edges, set apart
H0678.detail:
1. The word designates the most eminent, most worthy individuals of a community. In Exodus 24:11, after receiving the Law at Sinai, God does not strike "the elite of the children of Israel": these are the seventy elders and Moses, the leaders and notables of the people, whom God treats with distinction by inviting them to eat and drink in His presence.
2. The word can also describe what is located at the extremities, far from the center. In Isaiah 41:9, God tells His servant (Israel or Cyrus) that He has "called you from a distant land": the image is that of the ends of the earth, the far edges, away from the heart of the empire.
H0678.origine: The Hebrew word אָצִיל (atsil) comes from a root meaning "to set apart, separate, remove." The elite are those who stand out, who are separated from the common. The same word can describe what is spatially separated, that is, distant or marginal. This duality of meaning—social on one side, spatial on the other—reflects a common image: being "set apart," either by dignity or by distance.
H0678.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible. In Exodus 24:11, it refers to the spiritual leaders of Israel whom God honors at the conclusion of the Sinai covenant. In Isaiah 41:9, the same word changes context and takes on the meaning of "distant": God reminds His exiled people that He has called them from the ends of the earth. This versatility shows that the word retains its basic image—a separation, a distinction—while applying it to different realities depending on the context.
H0678.portee: For the reader, this word reminds us that God distinguishes His people and His servants, not by chance, but by a deliberate choice. Whether one is the elite of a nation or exiled at the edges, one never escapes God's gaze and call. This is a reason for confidence: those whom God chooses remain under His protection and attention, no matter how far they may be.

sens: Hollow or hollow part of the body where the arm attaches to the shoulder
Area where two architectural or structural elements meet and connect
H0679.detail:
1. The armpit is the hollow of the body located under the shoulder, where the arm joins the rest of the body. In Jeremiah 38:12, when Ebed-Melech helps Jeremiah escape from the pit, he asks him to pass worn rags "under your armpits" to pull him up by the rope: these are the two hollows under the arms that allow someone to be safely hoisted. In Ezekiel 13:18, the word refers to the same area of the body, but this time figuratively: the false prophetesses make "pads for all armpits," probably amulets or talismans intended to protect this area, imagined as vulnerable or important for health.
2. The word can also refer to the place where two elements meet and connect, like a joint. In Ezekiel 41:8, it describes the "great" cubits of the side chambers of the temple: this term refers to the junction area, the dimension of the structural connection between the different parts of the building.
H0679.origine: This Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes the idea of "joining" or "uniting." Its basic meaning is joint-related: it designates a point where two elements meet and unite — whether it is the human body (where the arm unites with the shoulder) or an architectural structure (where elements join together). The image is one of a link, a connection between two parts.
H0679.emploi: This word appears three times in the Hebrew Bible, always in contexts describing a point of physical meeting. In Jeremiah 38:12, it is concrete and practical: the armpits are the physical means to hoist Jeremiah. In Ezekiel 13:18, the word remains anatomical but takes on a religious tone: the false prophetesses exploit people's fears by selling talismans meant to protect them. In Ezekiel 41:8, the context is purely architectural: the word describes a structural dimension of the temple, the height of the junctions. The word thus has a small number of biblical uses, but they reveal its versatility: anatomical, magical-religious, and constructive.
H0679.portee: This word reminds us that the human body — in its concrete vulnerability — was at the heart of biblical concerns: the armpits are the point through which one can save or harm someone. For the believer, recognizing these physical realities without seeking magical solutions (like the pads of the false prophetesses) is a form of trust: it is in God, not in amulets, that true protection is found.

sens: Set aside, keep for oneself without giving or sharing
Take a part of something to use elsewhere
Desire or want to possess something
Closed space or separate compartment
H0680.detail:
1. To retain primarily means to reserve something, to hold it back instead of distributing or delivering it. Esau asks his father: "Have you not reserved a blessing for me?" (Genesis 27:36) — his blessing had been retained by his brother Jacob, taken away from him.
2. To retain can also mean to withhold or extract a part of a whole to use elsewhere. God tells Moses: "I will take of the spirit that is upon you, and I will put it upon them" (Numbers 11:17) — the Lord takes a portion of Moses' spiritual gift to give to the elders.
3. By extension, to retain means to desire or covet, to want to keep for oneself. The Preacher confesses: "Whatever my eyes desired, I did not keep from them" (Ecclesiastes 2:10) — he retained, kept for himself everything his heart wished for.
4. In an architectural context, to retain refers to a room or closed space, a part held back or separated from a building. Ezekiel describes the "chambers" of the temple (Ezekiel 42:6), distinct and reserved interior rooms.
H0680.origine: The Hebrew verb אָצַל comes from a root that expresses the idea of setting aside, separating, keeping in reserve. This root evokes the action of retaining something for oneself, not letting it go. It belongs to a family of words expressing separation and distinction.
H0680.emploi: This verb appears five times in the Hebrew biblical text. In Genesis 27:36, it describes the retained or taken blessing. In Numbers 11:17 and 11:25, it expresses divine withholding: God "takes" of the Spirit that rests upon Moses to give it to the elders, an image of sharing the spiritual gift. In Ecclesiastes 2:10, the term takes on a tone of covetousness: the man retains for himself everything his heart desires. In Ezekiel 42:6, it designates the chambers of the temple, separate and distinct interior spaces. The word thus covers the idea of retaining, setting aside, or compartmentalizing.
H0680.portee: This word reminds us that God's blessings are not to be selfishly hoarded. Esau loses his blessing because Jacob retained it for himself; in contrast, God "takes" of His Spirit to share generously. The text invites us to examine whether we are retaining the goods, talents, or graces we have received, or if we are putting them to the service of others, as God does.

sens: in immediate proximity, in direct neighborhood
placed or situated next to something
attached to, united with, in contact with
who stands beside someone, who accompanies them
H0681.detail: 1. The word first describes spatial proximity: being very close to someone or something, in their immediate neighborhood. When Gen 39:10 says that Potiphar's wife spoke "near" Joseph, it means she was constantly close to him, within reach. 2. It can refer to what is placed or attached beside something: Deuteronomy 16:21 forbids fixing an idol "beside" the altar of the Lord, thus directly in proximity. 3. The word also expresses the idea of being united or contiguous, like the wheels of the cherubim that moved "beside" them in Ezekiel (Ezekiel 10:16), not separated but moving together. 4. By extension, it describes one who remains "near" someone, who stays by their side, who assists or accompanies them in a relationship of constant presence.
H0681.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of physical proximity and contiguity. It is related to words describing junction, assembly, and presence beside. It is a very concrete word in the Hebrew language for situating things in space relative to one another.
H0681.emploi: This word appears 57 times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in narrative prose and spatial description. It is very frequent in Genesis (stories of Joseph), in the books of Kings and Chronicles (description of the temple and royal court), and abundantly in Ezekiel (visions of the temple and cherubim). Its main translations in French ("near," "side," "beside") show that the meaning remains stable: it always designates a relationship of proximity. Sometimes it implies a notion of support ("beside" when assisting someone), sometimes a simple spatial juxtaposition ("next to").
H0681.portee: This word reminds us that presence matters: being near someone establishes a living relationship, an accompaniment. In faith, it evokes the promise that God tells us: "I will always be with you," a reassuring proximity. It also teaches us to measure the value of faithful presence beside a person — much more than mere distance.

sens: A man from the tribe of Benjamin during the divided monarchy
H0682A.detail: Atsel is a Benjaminite descendant of Saul and Jonathan. He appears in the genealogy of Benjamin recorded twice in the first book of Chronicles (1 Chronicles 8 and 9). He is the son of Binea and the father of six sons: Azrikam, Bocru, Ismaël, Schearia, Abdias, and Hanan (1 Chronicles 8:37-38). His brothers were Rapha and Éleasa. This genealogy places him in the time of the divided monarchy.
H0682A.origine: The name Atsel means "reserved" or "set apart." It is a Hebrew name from the monarchical period that may indicate a certain distinction or separation. Atsel belongs to the lineage of Saul and Jonathan, prominent families of Benjamin.
H0682A.emploi: Atsel is mentioned only in the first book of Chronicles, twice: first in 1 Chronicles 8:37-38, and then in 1 Chronicles 9:43-44, where the same genealogy is repeated. These two identical occurrences show the importance that the author of Chronicles attached to the genealogy of Benjamin after the exile. Atsel figures as an essential link in the genealogical chain connecting Saul to the post-exilic period, and his six sons underscore the prosperity of his family branch.

sens: A place located near Jerusalem, mentioned in the prophecies of Zechariah
H0682B.detail: Atzel is a location near Jerusalem, the exact whereabouts of which are unknown today. Its Hebrew name suggests the idea of proximity or reserve. It is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Zechariah 14:5, in the context of the flight of the inhabitants during a great earthquake. This prophetic passage describes an eschatological event where a mountain valley will extend to Atzel.
H0682B.origine: The Hebrew word אָצֵל (atzel) carries the idea of proximity or that which is set aside. Although the precise etymology is debated among scholars, this toponym refers to a real geographical location in the region of Jerusalem, likely a village or locality in the vicinity of the capital.
H0682B.emploi: Atzel appears only once in the entirety of Scripture, in Zechariah 14:5. This passage is part of the conclusion of the book of Zechariah, in an eschatological prophecy concerning the coming of the Lord and the events that will accompany His return. The mention of Atzel serves as a geographical marker to describe the extent and scope of the earthly changes that will occur at that time.

sens: A man from the tribe of Judah during the divided monarchy, father of the scribe Shaphan
H0683.detail: Atsalia is a man from the time of the divided kingdom. He is known as the father of Shaphan, an important scribe who served King Josiah during the religious reform. Atsalia is mentioned twice to genealogically situate Shaphan: in 2 Kings 22:3, King Josiah sends "Shaphan the secretary, son of Atsalia, son of Meshullam," and in 2 Chronicles 34:8, the same Shaphan "son of Atsalia" is found in a similar mission of temple repair.
H0683.origine: The Hebrew name means "the Lord has set apart" or "the Lord has reserved." It expresses the idea that God has separated or predestined this person. It is a theophoric construction (containing the name of God) common in Hebrew.
H0683.emploi: Atsalia appears only twice in the Bible, always in the context of King Josiah's reform (around 620 B.C.). His importance primarily lies in the role of his son Shaphan, who was a key player in this reform: he discovered the Book of the Law in the temple and reported this discovery to the king. Atsalia thus represents a family of scribes and trusted statesmen during the decline of the kingdom of Judah.

sens: Son of Jesse and older brother of David
Member of the tribe of Judah during the united monarchy
H0684G.detail:
1. Otsem is one of the sons of Jesse, the father of David. He appears in the genealogy of Jesse's children as the sixth son, David being the seventh. He thus belongs to the same sibling group as the one who will become king of Israel.
2. Otsem is a man of the tribe of Judah who lived during the time when Israel was a united kingdom, probably under the reign of Saul or at the beginning of David's reign. Few details are given about his personal life or actions.
H0684G.origine: The name Otsem comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to hasten" or "to press," suggesting the idea of promptness or eagerness. The traditional meaning of the name, "I will hasten them" or "he will hasten them," expresses a quick and decisive action, although the name is found only once in the entire Bible.
H0684G.emploi: Otsem is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 2:15, where he appears in the genealogical list of Jesse's children. This mention occurs in the context of the census of the descendants of Judah established at the time of the united monarchy, probably under David. Although Otsem is a son of Jesse and thus a brother of David, no particular action or event is attributed to him in the biblical texts that have come down to us.

sens: Son of Jerachmeel and older brother of David
A man of the tribe of Judah during the united monarchy
H0684H.detail:
1. Otsem is the son of Jerachmeel, himself the eldest son of Hezron, and belongs to the genealogical lineage of Judah. He is the brother of Ram, Buna, Oren, Ahijah, and Onam, and he is the elder brother of David. His name appears in the genealogical register of God's people, anchoring his place in the history of Israel.

2. A minor historical figure, Otsem lived during the time of the united monarchy (before or at the beginning of David's reign). His existence is known only through a mention in 1 Chronicles 2:25, where he is listed among the descendants of Judah who formed the great families of the people.
H0684H.origine: The name Otsem literally means "I will hasten them" or "I will hurry," evoking the idea of speed or eagerness. It is an ancient Hebrew name formed from a verbal root. This name reflects the common practice in Semitic cultures of Israel to form proper names from verbs, often expressing a parental wish or aspiration.
H0684H.emploi: Otsem is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 2:25. He appears in the genealogy of the tribe of Judah, listed among the sons of Jerachmeel, alongside his brothers. This unique mention indicates that the Bible is only interested in Otsem to situate David within his family genealogy, without reporting any event or particular detail of his life. His genealogical role was important for establishing the legitimacy of the Davidic royal line.

sens: a metal ornament worn on the wrist or ankle
a chain or ring of precious metal signifying status or dignity
H0685.detail:
1. The bracelet is a metal ornament, usually made of gold or silver, worn around the wrist or ankle. It is a decorative object, often beautiful and precious. When the Israelites took spoils from Midian, they brought bracelets among the gold offerings to the Lord (Numbers 31:50).
2. The bracelet can also signify an important position or dignity: it is a badge of power or nobility. The Amalekite soldier who seizes the bracelet of King Saul along with his diadem shows that he covets the symbols of his royalty (2 Samuel 1:10).
H0685.origine: The Hebrew word אֶצְעָדָה (etsadah) is formed from a root that expresses the idea of attaching or binding. The bracelet is thus literally "that which surrounds" or "that which binds" the wrist or ankle. It is a very ancient decorative object, worn by prominent figures and warriors to mark their status.
H0685.emploi: The word appears twice in the Bible. In Numbers 31:50, after the victory against Midian, the gold bracelets are listed among the treasures to be offered to the Lord for atonement. In 2 Samuel 1:10, the bracelet of King Saul, taken with the diadem, symbolizes the marks of his royal power. In both cases, it is a precious and prestigious object.
H0685.portee: The bracelet reminds us that ornaments and material wealth, even the most precious, must be consecrated to God. It also illustrates that the external signs of power — diadem and bracelet — do not protect the one who wears them from defeat and death.

sens: To gather and keep things in large quantities
To accumulate goods, wealth
To entrust something to someone for safekeeping
H0686.detail:
1. To gather and keep things in large quantities: this is the concrete image of collecting objects and storing them. Hezekiah had amassed the treasures of his house over the years, and God announced that everything would be taken away to Babylon (Isaiah 39:6).
2. To accumulate goods, wealth, often in an unjust or dishonest manner: the palaces accumulate the products of violence and theft (Amos 3:10), while the impure gains of Tyre will not be piled up but consecrated to God (Isaiah 23:18).
3. To entrust something to someone, charging them to preserve and manage it: Nehemiah entrusted the oversight of the storerooms and distributions to trustworthy men (Nehemiah 13:13).
H0686.origine: The Hebrew verb אָצַר comes from a root that expresses the idea of reserving, storing. The basic notion is that of guarding, of deposit: one gathers to preserve, one entrusts for safekeeping. It is a verb that implies an intention of conservation and control.
H0686.emploi: This verb appears 5 times in the Hebrew Bible. It is first used for human wealth: Hezekiah had amassed the treasures of his fathers (2 Kings 20:17; Isaiah 39:6, parallel passages). It also describes unjust accumulation: the powerful pile up in their homes the fruits of violence (Amos 3:10). Finally, it can mean 'to entrust to': Nehemiah entrusts the administration of the temple storerooms to faithful men (Nehemiah 13:13). The context often shows a moral tension: to gather can be natural, but the result is fragile (taken into exile) or guilty (accumulated through plunder).
H0686.portee: This word invites reflection on our accumulations. The Bible does not condemn having possessions, but it reminds us that everything we 'gather' is fragile and temporary: God can take it back. It also warns against accumulation obtained through injustice. Finally, it values faithful trust: to entrust to others is to recognize that we truly possess nothing and that faithful management is better than jealous possession.

sens: Horite chief, son of Seir, living in the time of the Patriarchs
H0687.detail: Etser is a Horite chief mentioned in the genealogy of the descendants of Seir, the ancestor of the Horites who inhabited the land of Edom before the conquest. He is one of the seven sons of Seir (Genesis 36:21), alongside Lotan, Shobal, Zibeon, Anah, Dishon, and Dishan. Etser himself has three sons: Bilhan, Zaavan, and Akan (Genesis 36:27). He appears twice in the list of Horite chiefs (Genesis 36:21 and 36:30), indicating his importance in the social and political structure of the Horites of that time.
H0687.origine: The name Etser means 'treasure' in Hebrew. It designates one of the chiefs of the Horites, a people established in Edom before the arrival of the Edomites. His name and genealogy are preserved in the biblical records of God's people, testifying to the history of the peoples who occupied the promised land.
H0687.emploi: Etser is mentioned five times in the Hebrew Bible: four times in Genesis (36:21, 36:27, 36:30) and once in Chronicles (1:38 and 1:42). Each occurrence appears in genealogical lists that enumerate the descendants of Seir and the Horite chiefs. These lists serve to establish the identity of the ancient peoples of the land of Edom and to show how the geography and peoples of Canaan were organized before the time of Israel. Etser never intervenes in a narrative or event: he is only identified by his lineage (son of Seir, father of Bilhan, Zaavan, and Akan).

sens: Precious stone of a bright and sparkling red
Red glow or gleam, comparable to fire
H0688.detail:
1. The escarboucle is a precious stone of bright red color, characterized by its intense and sparkling brilliance. In the prophetic vision of Isaiah (54:12), it is among the building materials of glorified Jerusalem, highlighting its symbolic role as a stone of great value and beauty.
2. The word also evokes the visual quality of this gem: a sparkle, a fiery glow that shines like fire. It is this character of brilliance and luminous warmth that gives the stone its name.
H0688.origine: The Hebrew word אֶקְדָּח (eqdach) comes from a root meaning 'to ignite' or 'to burn', hence the image of flame and bright luster. Its name itself describes the visual impression it produces: a gem that seems to shine and sparkle like fire. In biblical Hebrew, it is one of the twelve stones of the high priest's breastplate (Exodus 28), called carbuncle or escarboucle in ancient versions.
H0688.emploi: The word appears only once in Isaiah 54:12, in a passage that depicts the glorified beauty of the future and restored Jerusalem. Here, the escarboucle is a symbolic building stone, listed alongside rubies and other precious stones. It represents the inexhaustible wealth, incomparable beauty, and divine glory that will characterize the new Jerusalem. It is a poetic and visionary term rather than an ordinary-use stone.
H0688.portee: The escarboucle invites the reader to contemplate the incomparable beauty of the promised celestial and restored Jerusalem. It symbolizes divine splendor and the final redemption that God will offer to His people. This gem detail encourages the believer to set their gaze on God's eternal promises, far beyond the temporal beauties of the present world.

sens: Wild animal resembling a goat, with long and curved horns
Animal whose meat the Law permits to eat
H0689.detail:
1. The bouquetin is a mountain animal, robust and agile, resembling a domestic goat but living in the wild. It has impressive, long horns that curve backward. It is a natural inhabitant of the rocky regions of the ancient Near East (Deuteronomy 14:5).
2. In the Law given to Israel, the bouquetin is among the clean animals that can be consumed. Moses indeed lists in Deuteronomy 14:5 a list of animals permitted at the Israelites' table: the deer, the gazelle, the doe, and the bouquetin are mentioned together, indicating that these wild beasts were not only known but also hunted and eaten by God's people.
H0689.origine: The Hebrew word aqo specifically designates this camelid or mountain animal of caprine type. The term comes from an ancient root describing the liveliness and agility of the animal. It should not be confused with other herbivorous animals: the domestic goat, the gazelle, or the antelope have different names in Hebrew.
H0689.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Deuteronomy 14:5, where Moses conveys to Israel the list of clean animals that may be eaten according to the Law. This unique presence shows that the bouquetin was well known to the Hebrew people to be cited immediately, alongside other prestigious game such as the deer and the gazelle. Its classification among the permitted animals indicates that it was neither impure nor dangerous for consumption.
H0689.portee: This verse reminds us that God knows and controls all creatures, even the wild animals of distant mountains. By allowing the consumption of the bouquetin, the Law acknowledges God's creation in its diversity and shows that the Lord provides for the needs of the people through the natural resources of the promised land.

sens: Son of Ithran, of the tribe of Asher
H0690.detail: Ara is a man of the tribe of Asher mentioned only once in the Bible, during the time of the divided monarchy. He is the son of Ithran and the brother of Jephunné and Pispa (1 Chronicles 7:38). It is a genealogical name that fits into the succession of the descendants of Asher, one of the twelve tribes of Israel.
H0690.origine: The name Ara means 'lion' in Hebrew, evoking strength and power. This name was borne by several characters in the Old Testament, but this one is specifically identified by his genealogy: son of Ithran, descendant of Asher.
H0690.emploi: Ara appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 7:38, in a genealogical list of the tribe of Asher. There he is listed with his brothers Jephunné and Pispa as sons of Ithran. This mention is part of the genealogical records that the Old Testament preserves to establish the lineage of the tribes of Israel, particularly important after the Exile.

sens: Man of remarkable courage and strength
Valiant and courageous warrior
H0691.detail:
1. The word designates a man who stands out for his physical courage and strength in battle. He is one who faces danger without fear and displays remarkable warrior power. In Isaiah 33:7, the "heroes" cry out, which evokes military leaders or warriors who take the lead in battles.
2. In a broader sense, it refers to the valiant man, one who inspires respect and fear through his authority and ability to lead to victory. The prophetic context of Isaiah shows these important figures in a moment of crisis, full of power but also of distress.
H0691.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes strength and courage. Its primary meaning refers to the image of the powerful warrior, one who rises up or dominates through his valor. Although the exact etymology is debated among scholars, the word fits within the family of Hebrew terms for figures of authority and strength.
H0691.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Isaiah 33:7. It designates high-ranking figures—probably leaders or diplomats—in a prophetic oracle announcing judgment and the restoration of Judah. The context shows these "heroes" in distress, crying out and weeping bitterly, which emphasizes that even human strength and courage are insufficient in the face of God's judgments.
H0691.portee: This passage reminds us that human valor and power, even those of the greatest warriors or highest dignitaries, remain fragile and powerless before the will of God. For the Christian, it is an invitation not to place trust in the strength of men, but to seek security in God alone, who is the true hero and who alone can save.

sens: Son of Gad, ancestor of a family of Israel
Member of the family of Ariel, one of the twelve tribes
H0692.detail:
1. Ariel is a man from the tribe of Gad, one of the twelve sons of this latter. He is mentioned for the first time in Genesis 46:16, when Jacob goes down to Egypt with his entire family. His name means "lion of God," evoking strength and divine presence.
2. The Arielites are the descendants of this Ariel, forming a family within the tribe of Gad. In Numbers 26:17, at the time of the census of the tribes before entering Canaan, this family is counted among the families of Gad, showing that Ariel's descendants prospered during the forty years in the desert.
H0692.origine: The name Ariel literally means "lion of God" in Hebrew, composed of "ariel" (lion) and the name of God. It is a common theophoric name in Israel, expressing divine protection and strength. Ariel appears as one of the sons of Gad, whose name itself means "good fortune." These names reflect the hopes and faith of the patriarchs in God.
H0692.emploi: Ariel is mentioned twice in the Bible, only in the genealogical lists of Israel. He first appears in Genesis 46:16 during Jacob's descent into Egypt, where the seven sons of Gad are listed. Then, in Numbers 26:17, he is cited again in the census of Israelite families in the desert, where the Arielites form a distinct family among the tribes. These mentions show the importance of genealogies in establishing the identity and heritage of the tribes of Israel.
H0692.portee: The name of Ariel and his descendants remind us of God's faithfulness to Jacob's family. Despite centuries of slavery in Egypt and the trials of the desert, the families of Israel multiplied, fulfilling the divine promise. This encourages the believer to trust in God's promises, even when circumstances seem unfavorable.

sens: To lie in wait to surprise or attack someone
Group of warriors placed in a secret position to spring upon the enemy
Trap set against a person to kill or harm them
Hidden ruse or scheme
H0693.detail:
1. The literal meaning is to lie in ambush, hidden, waiting for the moment to strike: it is the attitude of the hunter or soldier who conceals himself to surprise. Joshua 8:19 illustrates this well: the men in ambush remained hidden until a signal, then sprang out "quickly."
2. An ambush is also the group of people themselves posted in secret. Judges 20:37 speaks of the "men in ambush" who swiftly fell upon the city: it is a combat detachment hidden in the vicinity.
3. The word takes on a figurative meaning to designate the moral trap or evil laid against someone. Proverbs 1:18 denounces those who "set ambushes" against their own blood, meaning those who secretly plot to harm.
4. By extension, any hidden ruse, any concealed scheme to deceive or attack: Proverbs 12:6 speaks of "words" laid in ambush, like verbal traps.
H0693.origine: The Aramaic verb אָרַב comes from a root that evokes the idea of crouching, hiding in the shadows. The derived noun עָרֵב (areb) designates the ambush itself. The word belongs to the family of words related to watch and hostile vigilance: it paints the image of a predator that becomes invisible before striking. This ancient military strategy (posting hidden men to surprise the enemy) was common in the Middle East.
H0693.emploi: The word occurs 39 times in the Bible, especially in the war narratives of Joshua and Judges. It first describes concrete military tactics: Joshua 8 reports how the army of Israel laid ambushes to retake Ai; Judges 20 speaks of ambushes set in the war of Gibeah. The word also applies to ordinary watches: the people of Gaza in "ambush" awaited Samson at the gate (Judges 16:2). In Proverbs (six occurrences), the meaning becomes moral and spiritual: ambushes become ruses, plots, or even temptations to sin (Proverbs 7:12 speaks of a woman who "sets the ambush"). Lamentations (3:10; 4:19) uses it poetically to express how God seems to have laid traps in Jerusalem.
H0693.portee: This word reminds us that evil often operates hidden, in secret, like a watcher who conceals himself. The Christian reader recognizes the biblical image of sin and temptation that lurk (1 Peter 5:8 speaks of the devil who "roams around us"). But the word also teaches that vigilance and military strategy are legitimate against the true enemy. Finally, Proverbs warns that our own words and desires can turn into ambushes against ourselves.

sens: City of Judah near Hebron
H0694.detail: Arab is a city located in the territory of Judah, near Hebron. It is mentioned only once in the Bible during the enumeration of cities assigned to the tribe of Judah at the conquest of Canaan (Joshua 15:52).
H0694.origine: The Hebrew name אֲרָב (Arab) literally means "ambush" or "trap," but it designates here a specific locality in the Jewish territory. The etymology suggests that the place got its name from a geographical feature—perhaps a spot where one could hide or ambush—or from a historical event related to an ambush.
H0694.emploi: Arab appears only once in the Bible in Joshua 15:52, in the list of cities that Joshua distributed to the tribe of Judah after the conquest of Canaan. It is among a series of localities in the Judean mountain range, which situates its geographical location in the heights of Judah. This cadastral mention shows that it was a recognized and administered settlement within the kingdom of Judah.

sens: hidden place where an animal retreats
ambush site, strategic hiding place
H0695.detail:
1. The den is the place where a wild animal retreats to rest or protect itself — its lair, its natural refuge. It is a closed, secret place, shielded from view. Job 37:8 refers to it when it speaks of the wild animal that "withdraws into a cave, and lies down in its den": this is its space for rest and safety.
2. By extension, it is also a place from which one watches for the enemy, a strategic hiding place from which to strike by surprise. Job 39:2 speaks of animals "lying in wait in their den": the image is one of a place of waiting and observation before the attack.
H0695.origine: The Hebrew word אֶרֶב comes from a root that evokes the idea of hiding, concealing, watching in secret. The starting image is one of darkness and invisible waiting. The den is therefore primarily a place where one withdraws from sight, and by extension a hidden observation post.
H0695.emploi: This word appears only twice in the Bible, both in the book of Job, in chapters 37 and 39. These two passages describe the behavior of wild animals: the first refers to their natural retreat for rest, the second to their position of waiting before the attack. The biblical usage remains concrete and limited to the animal world, never being applied to human behavior in the preserved usages.
H0695.portee: This word reminds us that all of nature, even in its fiercest creatures, obeys ordered rhythms and behaviors. For the reader, it emphasizes how God knows and governs the secret habits of wild animals, which expands the wonder of creation and divine providence.

sens: Ambush, hidden place from which one waits for the enemy to attack by surprise
Ruse, treachery, hidden intention to do harm
H0696.detail:
1. The trap primarily evokes a military ambush: soldiers hide in wait to spring out unexpectedly and strike the enemy. It is a setup, a war stratagem where the secrecy of the place and the moment decides the victory (Hosea 7:6).
2. In a figurative sense, the trap denotes moral cunning, treachery hidden in the heart. In particular, the deceptive word: a mouth that promises peace while the heart prepares evil, like soldiers hiding before striking (Jeremiah 9:8). It is the betrayal of the confidant, the close one who says "peace" and thinks "disaster."
H0696.origine: The Hebrew word אֹ֫רֶב (orev) comes from a root that means "to hide," "to lie in wait." The basic image is that of a warrior lurking in darkness, concealed, who is watching. The family of the word includes terms designating ambush, hiding place, and by extension, everything that is hidden and malevolent. It is a concrete word that extends to the moral sphere.
H0696.emploi: The word appears twice in the French Old Testament, in two passages that illustrate its extension from military to moral. In Jeremiah 9:8, the tongue of liars is compared to traps: it conceals a hostile intention under sweet words. In Hosea 7:6, hearts "apply to snares" their destructive intention, like an oven prepared to burn. The word is always linked to a hidden intention, to a concealed danger that waits for the moment to strike.
H0696.portee: This word teaches the believer to beware of hidden treachery, especially that which comes from sweet words. Jesus will also warn his disciples against false prophets who speak of peace. Recognizing these spiritual traps helps the faithful not to be seduced by elegant lies and to cultivate transparency of heart.

sens: Destructive insect with an elongated body, powerful legs, that jumps and flies
Swarm of locusts devastating crops
Insignificant, fragile, and unimportant being or thing
Sudden disappearance, annihilation
H0697.detail:
1. The locust is a well-known insect in the Middle East and North Africa, capable of destroying crops in a short time. In Egypt, during the eighth plague, God sends locusts in such great numbers that they cover the sky and devour every living plant (Exodus 10:4, 10:14). The Law of Moses permits their consumption for the Hebrews (Leviticus 11:22), acknowledging that they are part of the edible insects.
2. A single locust causes little damage, but gathered in countless swarms, they become a calamity. Joel describes how locusts, in various forms, successively devour the crops (Joel 1:4), and the Psalms speak of a plague where they ravage the harvests of humans (Psalms 78:46, 105:34).
3. In figurative language, the fragility and insignificance of the locust make it an image of smallness: Jesus will say that whoever receives a child in the name of Christ receives him (Matthew 18:5), thus reversing the order of greatness in the world. The insect, despite its multitude in swarms, remains vulnerable.
4. The unpredictable and sudden nature of a swarm of locusts symbolizes a rapid disappearance or annihilation. Man before God may also seem unstable: "I have become like the locust" (Psalms 109:23), expressing the precariousness of human existence.
H0697.origine: The Hebrew word אַרְבֶּה (arbeh) literally designates this jumping insect recognizable by its long hind legs. The root evokes the idea of multiplicity and fertility: a single locust quickly begets a multitude. The word is related to terms meaning "to grow" or "to multiply," as locusts reproduce in considerable numbers. In the Hebrew Bible, this word retains its primary concrete meaning but is charged with strong symbolic value: manifestation of divine power, mark of judgment, image of human fragility.
H0697.emploi: The word arbeh appears 21 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the accounts of the plagues of Egypt (Exodus 10), in the texts of blessing and cursing (Deuteronomy 28:38), and in the prophetic books. Exodus 10:4-14 reports how God sends locusts as the eighth plague, transforming the Egyptian landscape. Deuteronomy 28:38 lists the locust among the plagues striking the one who disobeys the Covenant. The Psalms and Joel use the plague of locusts to speak of divine justice and judgment on Israel. Proverbs 30:27 mentions that "the locusts have no king," ironically praising their natural organization. The word retains its primary concrete meaning everywhere: it is always the real insect that devastates, never a mere abstract symbol.
H0697.portee: The locust teaches the biblical reader that the powers of creation obey God and serve his purposes. Seeing locusts ravaging the land is not a mere natural disaster, but a sign of divine judgment and his sovereign right over human history. Conversely, the fragility of the locust reminds man, even seemingly powerful, of his own smallness before God. Finally, swarms of locusts illustrate how God can accomplish his will through humble and natural means, without resorting to brute force, teaching the believer a greater trust in divine providence.

sens: Ruse, stratagème, manœuvre destinée à tromper ou à nuire
Habileté malveillante mise en œuvre par les mains ou par l'action
H0698.detail:
1. The word denotes a ruse or a stratagem — a way of doing that aims to deceive or obtain something through deception. It is a calculated, dishonest action. In Isaiah 25:11, this term characterizes the proud prowess of Moab, who believes he can swim out of submersion by his own strength: God "frustrates the craft of his hands," showing that human skill, even when it seems very adept, can do nothing against His will.
